Entre idosos com perda importante de visão, estudos relatam que 10% a 40% passam por isso. O número real é incerto, porque muitos não contam a ninguém, com medo de serem tomados por loucos.

fontes.trecho: Visual release hallucinations, also known as Charles Bonnet syndrome (CBS), are a type of psychophysical visual disturbance in which a person with partial or severe blindness experiences visual hallucinations. First described by Charles Bonnet in 1760 [...] These can vary greatly in apparent size, sometimes "lilliputian" (smaller than normal) [...] Simple hallucinations often involve shapes, photopsias, and grid-like patterns. Complex hallucinations may depict silent, non-interactive figures, whether multitudes of people, animals, or surreal objects, that appear life-like, as well as highly detailed landscapes or objects. The most common hallucination is of faces or cartoons. Those affected understand that the hallucinations are not real, although in some cases, particularly when cognitive decline progresses, they may begin to perceive them as genuine. Hallucinations are purely visual [...] Among older adults (> 65 years) with significant vision loss, the prevalence of Charles Bonnet syndrome has been reported to be between 10% and 40% [...] Underreporting is thought to be a result of those with the condition being afraid to discuss the symptoms out of fear that they will be labeled of unsound mind. [...] The most commonly accepted theory for Charles Bonnet syndrome proposes that extreme visual impairment promotes sensory deafferentation, leading to disinhibition, thus resulting in sudden neural firings of the visual cortical regions. [...] The disease was first noted by the Swiss naturalist Charles Bonnet, who described the condition in 1760. He documented it in his 87-year-old grandfather who was nearly blind from cataracts in both eyes. [...] His hallucinations consisted of perceptions of men, women, birds, carriages, buildings, tapestries, physically impossible circumstances and scaffolding patterns. Even though his health was in good shape and he had an absence of any psychiatric disorders, the source of the hallucinations remained unknown. At forty years old, Charles Bonnet himself developed an unrevealed cause of severe vision loss and experienced the hallucinations.

gancho: Nos anos 1960, um estudo famoso concluiu que os San do Kalahari caíam pouco numa ilusão de óptica clássica e explicou isso pela falta de cantos retos ao redor. Hoje a ideia está desacreditada.
explicacao: A ilusão de Müller-Lyer, criada em 1889, faz duas linhas iguais parecerem de tamanhos diferentes conforme as pontas de seta apontem para dentro ou para fora. Na virada para o século 20, W. H. R. Rivers relatou que os nativos da ilha Murray, na Austrália, eram menos suscetíveis a ela do que os europeus. Em 1963, Marshall Segall, Donald Campbell e Melville Herskovits compararam várias populações: o erro médio ia de 1,4% a 20,3%, as três amostras de origem europeia foram as mais enganadas e os San, caçadores-coletores do Kalahari, as menos. Num artigo de 1966, com dezessete culturas, os autores atribuíram a diferença ao mundo "carpinteirado" das cidades, cheio de retas e ângulos retos, que treinaria a visão. Vieram resultados conflitantes: Gustav Jahoda não achou diferença entre membros de um mesmo povo africano no campo e na cidade, e um estudo de 1978 na Zâmbia achou os moradores urbanos mais suscetíveis. Hoje a hipótese é amplamente contestada. A ilusão funciona com linhas curvas e até com pontos no lugar das linhas. Crianças cegas a vida toda que fazem cirurgia para trocar o cristalino caem nela logo depois de começar a enxergar. E aves, peixes, répteis e insetos também parecem cair. Para os pesquisadores Dorsa Amir e Chaz Firestone, os estudos clássicos provavelmente refletem práticas hoje vistas como problemáticas, como descartar dados inconvenientes e não fazer os testes estatísticos adequados.

fontes.trecho: The illusion was devised by Franz Carl Müller-Lyer (1857–1916), a German sociologist, in 1889. Research suggests all humans are susceptible to the illusion across cultures. [...] Around the turn of the 20th century, W. H. R. Rivers wrote that indigenous people of the Australian Murray Island were less susceptible to the Müller-Lyer illusion than were Europeans. [...] In 1963, Segall, Campbell and Herskovitz compared susceptibility to four different visual illusions in three population samples of Caucasians, twelve of Africans, and one from the Philippines. For the Müller-Lyer illusion, the mean fractional misperception of the length of the line segments varied from 1.4% to 20.3%. The three European-derived samples were the three most susceptible samples, while the San foragers of the Kalahari desert were the least susceptible. [...] In their definitive paper of 1966, they investigated seventeen cultures and showed that people in different cultures differ substantially on how they experience the Müller-Lyer stimuli. They wrote that "European and American city dwellers have a much higher percentage of rectangularity in their environments than non-Europeans and so are more susceptible to that illusion." They also used the word "carpentered" for the environments that Europeans mostly live in - characterized by straight lines, right angles, and square corners. These conclusions were challenged in later work by Gustav Jahoda, who compared members of an African tribe living in a traditional rural environment with members of same group living in African cities. Here, no significant difference in susceptibility to the M-L illusion was found. Subsequent work by Jahoda suggested that retinal pigmentation may have a role in the differing perceptions on this illusion [...] A later study was conducted in 1978 by Ahluwalia on children and young adults from Zambia. Subjects from rural areas were compared with subjects from urban areas. The subjects from urban areas were shown to be considerably more susceptible to the illusion [...] The illusion appears to be experienced by all human beings seeing it, even those who have been blind. This suggests susceptibility to the illusion is neurologically constant across humans, and undermines hypothesis promulgated in the twentieth century proposing that susceptibility was culturally determined. Such hypotheses were based on research that suffered from poor methodology and contamination by false cultural assumptions. Non-human animals are also susceptible to the illusion. [...] The fins can point inwards to form an arrow "head" or outwards to form an arrow "tail". The line segment forming the shaft of the arrow with two tails is perceived to be longer than that forming the shaft of the arrow with two heads.

fontes.titulo: Why a Classic Psychology Theory about Vision Has Fallen Apart (Scientific American, 2025)
fontes.trecho: August 22, 2025 [...] psychologists in the 1960s had apparently discovered something remarkable about the illusion: only European and American urbanites fell for the trick. The illusion worked less well, or didn't work at all, on groups surveyed across Africa and the Philippines. [...] is now widely disputed, including by Amir herself. [...] The researchers theorized that the prevalence of carpentry features, such as rectangular spaces and right angles, trained the visual systems of people in more wealthy, industrialized cultures to perceive these angles in a way that make them more prone to the Müller-Lyer illusion. [...] For starters, the illusion still works when the lines are curved or even when there are no lines at all and dots take their place [...] Even more convincing, kids who have been blind their whole life and undergo lens replacement surgery are susceptible to the illusion shortly after gaining sight. And even some animals, such as birds, fish, reptiles, insects and nonhuman mammals, seem to fall for the trick. [...] these were the results of “research practices now recognized to be problematic by modern methodological standards (including discarding inconvenient data points, and failing to conduct appropriate statistical tests),” Amir and Firestone wrote.

gancho: No horizonte, a Lua parece bem maior do que no alto do céu, embora ali esteja um pouco mais longe de nós. A ilusão é conhecida desde a Antiguidade e ainda não tem uma explicação aceita por todos.
explicacao: Medida com instrumento, a Lua ocupa o mesmo ângulo no céu em qualquer altura, e fotos mostram o mesmo tamanho. Perto do horizonte ela está até cerca de 1,5% mais distante e, portanto, um tiquinho menor. Um teste caseiro: uma pedrinha de 8,4 milímetros, segurada com o braço esticado, cobre a Lua tanto no alto quanto no horizonte. Mesmo assim, a ilusão costuma aumentar o diâmetro aparente em cerca de 50%. Ptolomeu tentou explicá-la pela refração da atmosfera, e o astrônomo Cleomedes, por volta do ano 200, a atribuiu à refração e a mudanças na distância aparente. Entre 1011 e 1022, Ibn al-Haytham propôs que os objetos entre nós e o horizonte mudam a nossa noção de distância. Só no século 17 a ilusão passou a ser aceita como fenômeno psicológico. Hoje a pista mais forte é ver o terreno até o horizonte, e a explicação mais popular a compara à ilusão de Ponzo. Mesmo assim, o debate segue: um livro de 2002 que revisou as teorias concluiu que nenhuma saiu vitoriosa, e um livro de 2013 reuniu 19 capítulos de pesquisadores que chegam a conclusões diferentes.

fontes.trecho: The Moon illusion is the optical illusion of the Moon appearing larger near the horizon than it does higher up in the sky. It has been known since ancient times and recorded by various cultures. The illusion is seen also with other celestial objects (such as in a sunset or sunrise, and constellations) and remains inconclusively explained, with the ponzo illusion as a popular explanation. [...] The Moon is actually only about 1.5% farther away and thus smaller in angular size when at the horizon than when above. The angle that the diameter of the full Moon subtends at an observer's eye can be measured directly with a theodolite to show that it remains constant as the Moon rises or sinks in the sky. Photographs of the Moon at different elevations also show that its size remains the same. A simple way of demonstrating that the effect is an illusion is to hold a small pebble (say, 0.33 inches or 8.4 millimetres wide) at arm's length [...] The 2013 book The Moon Illusion, edited by Hershenson, offers 19 chapters written by various illusion researchers reaching different conclusions. After reviewing the many different explanations in their 2002 book The Mystery of the Moon Illusion, Ross and Plug conclude "No single theory has emerged victorious." They argue that the size of the illusion is variable, but is usually an apparent increase in diameter of about 50 percent. The most important factor is the sight of the terrain [...] Ptolemy attempted to explain the Moon illusion through atmospheric refraction in the Almagest [...] Similarly Cleomedes (about 200 A.D.), in his book on astronomy, ascribed the illusion both to refraction and to changes in apparent distance. In the Book of Optics (1011–1022 A.D.), Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) repeated refraction as an explanation, but also proposed a more detailed explanation based on intervening objects and apparent distance. [...] the Moon illusion came to be accepted as a psychological phenomenon in the 17th century.

gancho: Numa foto de rosto de cabeça para baixo, olhos e boca invertidos passam quase despercebidos. Desvire a foto, e o rosto fica grotesco. O truque foi criado em 1980 com uma foto de Margaret Thatcher.
explicacao: O criador foi o psicólogo Peter Thompson, da Universidade de York, que usou a foto da então primeira-ministra britânica, e por isso o fenômeno ficou conhecido como efeito Thatcher. Basta inverter verticalmente os olhos e a boca, deixando o resto do rosto como está. De cabeça para baixo, a alteração quase não se nota; na posição normal, salta aos olhos. A explicação mais aceita é que o cérebro tem processos especializados em rostos na posição de sempre. Para distinguir caras tão parecidas entre si, ele usaria tanto a configuração, ou seja, a relação entre os traços, quanto os detalhes de cada olho, nariz e boca. Há indícios de que macacos-rhesus e chimpanzés também caem no efeito, o que sugere que parte desse maquinário de rostos pode vir de um ancestral comum de mais de 30 milhões de anos. Já pessoas com prosopagnosia congênita, a dificuldade de reconhecer rostos, reagem bem menos à ilusão.

fontes.trecho: The Thatcher effect, or Thatcher illusion, is a phenomenon in which changes to facial features are difficult to detect when a face is upside-down, even though the same changes are obvious in an upright face. It is named after the then British prime minister Margaret Thatcher, on whose photograph the effect was first demonstrated. The effect was originally created in 1980 by Peter Thompson, professor of psychology at the University of York. [...] The second picture is altered so that the eyes and mouth are vertically flipped, though the changes are not immediately obvious until the image is viewed upright. The Thatcher effect is thought to be due to specific psychological cognitive modules involved in face perception which are tuned especially to upright faces. [...] It has been hypothesized that humans develop specific processes to differentiate between faces that rely as much on the configuration (the structural relationship between individual features on the face) as the details of individual face features, such as the eyes, nose and mouth. There is evidence that rhesus monkeys as well as chimpanzees experience the Thatcher effect, raising the possibility that some brain mechanisms involved in processing faces may have evolved in a common ancestor more than 30 million years ago. [...] However, people with congenital prosopagnosia have been shown to exhibit an overall much weaker response to the illusion compared to people without such condition.

gancho: Esconda a mão de alguém, ponha uma mão de borracha à vista e acaricie as duas com um pincel ao mesmo tempo: muita gente passa a sentir a falsa como sua. Hoje se discute quanto disso é sugestão.
explicacao: A ilusão da mão de borracha foi relatada em 1998 por Botvinick e Cohen. Quando a mão escondida e a falsa recebem pinceladas sincronizadas e na mesma direção, a pessoa começa a vivê-la como parte do corpo; se as pinceladas são desencontradas, não. Pedidas para apontar a própria mão, as cobaias costumam indicar a de borracha. Em exames de imagem, a sensação coincide com a ativação do córtex pré-motor. Quando a mão falsa é ameaçada com uma agulha, acende uma região ligada à expectativa de dor, e os voluntários reagiam puxando a mão verdadeira, que nunca esteve em perigo. Até macacos-rhesus caem no truque. Desde 2019, porém, Lush e colegas questionam a interpretação clássica. Num estudo com 353 participantes, a força da ilusão acompanhou a sugestionabilidade hipnótica de cada um, e eles argumentaram que as expectativas dos voluntários nunca foram bem controladas nesses experimentos e que podem explicar parte, ou até tudo, do efeito. Em 2022, Slater e Ehrsson responderam que os dados não sustentam essa conclusão e que o motor principal é a integração entre visão e tato.

fontes.trecho: The rubber hand illusion was originally reported by Botvinick and Cohen in 1998. [...] Subjects with normal brain function were positioned with their left hand hidden out of sight. They saw a lifelike rubber left hand in front of them. The experimenters stroked both the subjects hidden left hand and the visible rubber hand with a paintbrush. The experiment showed that if the two hands were stroked synchronously and in the same direction, the subjects began to experience the rubber hand as their own. When asked to use their right hand to point to their left hand, most of the time they pointed toward the rubber hand. If the real and rubber hands were stroked in different directions or at different times, the subjects did not experience the rubber hand as their own. [...] as the subjects began to experience the rubber hand as their own, in the premotor cortex [...] Then, threatened the rubber hand by making a stabbing movement toward it with a needle (not actually making contact with the rubber hand). MRI scans showed increase activity in a region of the brain called the anterior cingulate cortex that is normally activated when a person anticipates pain [...] The anticipation of the needle made the subjects react as if the rubber hand was their own, moving their real hand to avoid the needle even though it was never actually in danger. The rubber hand illusion can be induced in rhesus monkeys [...] In 2019, Lush et al., reported correlations between response to the rubber hand illusion and both response to imaginative suggestions in hypnosis and participant expectations for illusion experience and argued that body transfer illusions may be suggestion effects generated by participants' expectations. In 2020, Lush reported that demand characteristics (contextual cues which prime participant expectations) have not been controlled in rubber hand illusion experiments, and argued that existing reports of body transfer illusions may be entirely accounted for by suggestion effects. In 2022, Slater and Ehrsson argued that Lush's claims were not supported by the data and that the major factor driving the rubber hand illusion is multisensory integration.

fontes.titulo: Trait phenomenological control predicts experience of mirror synaesthesia and the rubber hand illusion (Nature Communications, 2020, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: In large sample studies (of 156, 404 and 353 participants), we report substantial relationships between hypnotisability and experimental measures of experiential change in mirror-sensory synaesthesia and the rubber hand illusion [...] we collected RHI and hypnotisability measures from 353 participants across groups [...] These embodiment effects may or may not be entirely attributable to demand characteristics and phenomenological control.

gancho: Toques rápidos perto do pulso e depois perto do cotovelo são sentidos como pulinhos subindo pelo braço, inclusive no meio, onde nada tocou. O efeito aparece até ao longo de um bastão apoiado nos dedos.
explicacao: É a ilusão do coelho cutâneo, descoberta no início dos anos 1970 por Frank Geldard e Carl Sherrick, da Universidade de Princeton. Eles compararam a sensação à de um coelho saltitando sobre a pele. Ela funciona melhor onde a pele distingue mal os pontos, como o antebraço, e só aparece se os toques vierem bem seguidos: com mais de cerca de 0,3 segundo entre eles, some. Os toques fantasmas ativam a mesma área do mapa sensorial do cérebro que toques reais ativariam. Quando voluntários apoiaram um bastão entre as pontas dos indicadores e receberam os toques por ele, sentiram os pulinhos ao longo do bastão, como se o objeto fizesse parte do corpo. Os mecanismos neurais exatos são desconhecidos. Um modelo estatístico reproduz bem o efeito supondo que o cérebro espera que estímulos na pele fiquem parados ou se movam devagar: diante de toques muito rápidos, conclui que eles estavam mais próximos do que estavam. Em 2009, pesquisadores da Philips mostraram uma jaqueta que aproveitava a ilusão para fazer sentir na pele cenas de filme com menos motores.

fontes.trecho: The cutaneous rabbit illusion (also known as cutaneous saltation and sometimes the cutaneous rabbit effect or CRE) is a tactile illusion evoked by tapping two or more separate regions of the skin in rapid succession. The illusion is most readily evoked on regions of the body surface that have relatively poor spatial acuity, such as the forearm. A rapid sequence of taps delivered first near the wrist and then near the elbow creates the sensation of sequential taps hopping up the arm from the wrist towards the elbow, although no physical stimulus was applied between the two actual stimulus locations. [...] The illusion was discovered by Frank Geldard and Carl Sherrick of Princeton University, in the early 1970s [...] Geldard and Sherrick likened the perception to that of a rabbit hopping along the skin, giving the phenomenon its name. [...] the illusion disappears if the temporal separation between taps exceeds about 0.3 seconds (300 milliseconds). [...] Another study showed that the illusory taps are associated with neural activity in the same area of the brain's sensory map that is activated by real taps to the skin. Nevertheless, the specific neural mechanisms that underlie the rabbit illusion are unknown. [...] When subjects supported a stick across their index fingertips and received the taps via the stick, they reported sensing the illusory taps along the stick. This suggests that the cutaneous rabbit effect involves not only the intrinsic somatotopic representation but also the representation of the extended body schema that results from body-object interactions. [...] In 2009, researchers of Philips Electronics demonstrated a jacket lined with actuator motors and designed to evoke various tactile sensations while watching a movie. The device takes advantage of the cutaneous rabbit illusion to reduce the number of actuators needed. [...] A Bayesian perceptual model closely replicates the cutaneous rabbit and other tactile spatiotemporal illusions. According to this model, brain circuitry encodes the expectation, acquired through sensory experience, that tactile stimuli tend to be stationary or to move only slowly. [...] The expectation that stimuli tend to move slowly results in the perceptual conclusion that rapidly successive stimuli are more likely to be closer together on the skin.

gancho: Pisque um ponto azul e, logo depois, um vermelho em outro lugar: muita gente vê um só ponto que anda e muda de cor no meio do caminho. Só que relatam ver a troca de cor antes de o ponto vermelho surgir.
explicacao: O efeito se chama phi colorido e foi descrito pelos psicólogos Paul Kolers e Michael von Grünau. Eles o investigaram para responder a uma pergunta do filósofo Nelson Goodman: o que acontece com a ilusão de movimento aparente, a mesma que faz uma sequência de imagens paradas parecer animada, quando as duas imagens têm cores diferentes? No experimento clássico, projeta-se um ponto azul no alto da tela e, em seguida, um vermelho embaixo. Com certas combinações de distância e intervalo, o espectador vê o primeiro ponto deslizar e mudar de cor bruscamente na metade do trajeto. Aí está o enigma: a troca é percebida num ponto do caminho em que o ponto vermelho ainda não foi mostrado, o que não poderia ser vivido de fato naquele instante. O filósofo Daniel Dennett usou o fenômeno em seu argumento contra o chamado materialismo cartesiano, e outros pesquisadores propõem explicações mais simples, de modo que a interpretação continua em disputa.

fontes.trecho: The color phi phenomenon is the fact that, when apparent motion is induced between objects with different colors, the color of the apparently moving object abruptly changes midway along the path. It is a perceptual illusion described by psychologists Paul Kolers and Michael von Grünau in which a disembodied perception of motion is produced by a succession of still images. [...] Kolers and von Grünau originally investigated the phenomenon in response to a question posed by the philosopher Nelson Goodman, who asked what the effect of the color change would have on the phi phenomenon. [...] The first image depicts a blue dot at the top of the frame. The second image depicts a red dot on the bottom of the frame. [...] At certain combinations of spacing and timing of the two images, a viewer will report a sensation of motion in the space between the two dots. The first spot will begin to appear to be moving, and will then "change color abruptly in the middle of its illusory path". [...] When asked to describe their experience, subjects report seeing the abrupt color change before the second dot is presented. However, it is impossible for a subject to actually experience the color change before the second dot has been presented. Philosopher Daniel Dennett utilizes the color phi phenomenon in his argument against a philosophy known as Cartesian materialism. Psychobiologist John Staddon contrasts a simple "new behaviorism" interpretation of color phi with Dennett and Kinsbourne's account. [...] Alternatively, phi can be explained without Dennett's argument.

gancho: Ponha um peso dentro de uma de três caixas de fósforos vazias. Erguida sozinha, ela parece mais pesada do que as três juntas, empilhadas com ela no topo. É a ilusão tamanho-peso.
explicacao: A ilusão foi demonstrada em experimento pelo médico francês Augustin Charpentier: entre dois objetos de mesma massa, o maior parece mais leve. Algo parecido acontece com material e cor: um recipiente de metal parece mais leve que um de madeira de mesmo tamanho e massa, e objetos escuros parecem mais pesados que claros. A primeira explicação era mecânica: esperando que o objeto grande pese mais, a pessoa o ergue com mais força, e ele sobe fácil demais. Mas a ilusão aparece também quando os objetos são apenas pousados sobre mãos apoiadas, sem levantamento nenhum. E estudos mostraram que a força usada para erguer se ajusta rápido à massa real, enquanto a ilusão continua. Por isso ela é vista como uma recalibração da percepção a partir do que se esperava. Há quem a chame de "anti-bayesiana", porque o cérebro daria peso demais à informação inesperada em vez de fazer uma média; outros pesquisadores acham que ela resulta de uma inferência ótima, só que mais complexa.

fontes.trecho: The size–weight illusion, also known as the Charpentier illusion, is named after the French physician Augustin Charpentier because he was the first to demonstrate the illusion experimentally. [...] The illusion occurs when a person underestimates the weight of a larger object (e.g. a box) when compared to a smaller object of the same mass. [...] Similar illusions occurs with differences in material and colour: metal containers feel lighter than wooden containers of the same size and mass, and darker objects feel heavier than brighter objects of the same size and mass. [...] An early explanation of these illusions was that people judge the weight of an object from its appearance and then lift it with a pre-determined force. They expect a larger object to be heavier and therefore lift it with greater force: the larger object is then lifted more easily than the smaller one, causing it to be perceived as lighter. This hypothesis was disproved by an experiment in which two objects of the same mass, same cross section, but different height were placed on observers' supported hands, and produced a passive size–weight illusion. Recent studies have also shown that the lifting force quickly adapts to the true mass of the objects, but the size–weight illusion remains. The illusion therefore cannot be explained by the manner of lifting, and must be due to some perceptual rescaling based on prior expectations. The rescaling has been described as sub-optimal (anti-Bayesian), in that the central nervous system integrates prior expectations with current proprioceptive information in a way that emphasises the unexpected information rather than taking an average of all information. It has also recently been suggested that the illusion may not be anti-Bayesian, but may instead rely on more complex yet still optimal inference processes than traditionally suggested. [...] It has also been demonstrated that, taking three empty matchboxes, and putting a weight in one of them, the weighted box lifted on its own feels heavier than all three boxes lifted together with the heavy one on top.

gancho: Há pessoas que veem cada letra com uma cor fixa. Num estudo com 6.588 delas nos EUA, ao menos 400 tinham as cores de um brinquedo: um conjunto de letras magnéticas da Fisher-Price fabricado de 1971 a 1990.
explicacao: É a sinestesia grafema-cor, em que letras ou números são percebidos como se tivessem cor própria. O estudo, publicado em 2015 por Witthoft e colegas, analisou as cores que 6.588 sinestetas americanos atribuíam às 26 letras em testes on-line. Os pesquisadores compararam essas escolhas com as cores do brinquedo, letras imantadas. Cerca de 6% dos participantes tinham dez ou mais letras com a mesma cor do conjunto, algo que, numa simulação com as respostas embaralhadas, ocorreu em menos de 0,009% dos casos. Para os nascidos em alguns períodos de cinco anos logo depois do lançamento, a fração chegou perto de 15%. E nenhum dos nascidos cinco anos ou mais antes da fabricação tinha as cores do brinquedo. Os autores frisam que o ímã foi a origem das combinações, não a causa da sinestesia: a única diferença aparente entre esses sinestetas e os outros era a exposição ao brinquedo. Ou seja, uma condição que parece inata pode ganhar o conteúdo do que a criança tinha na porta da geladeira.

fontes.titulo: Prevalence of learned grapheme-color pairings in a large online sample of synesthetes (PLoS ONE, 2015, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: 2015 Witthoft et al [...] In this paper we estimate the minimum prevalence of grapheme-color synesthetes with letter-color matches learned from an external stimulus, by analyzing a large sample of English-speaking grapheme-color synesthetes. We find that at least 6% (400/6588 participants) of the total sample learned many of their matches from a widely available colored letter toy. Among those born in the decade after the toy began to be manufactured, the proportion of synesthetes with learned letter-color pairings approaches 15% for some 5-year periods. Among those born 5 years or more before it was manufactured, none have colors learned from the toy. Analysis of the letter-color matching data suggests the only difference between synesthetes with matches to the toy and those without is exposure to the stimulus. [...] In this paper we examine the grapheme-color pairings of 6588 American synesthetes [...] 6588 synesthetes provided demographic information and performed tasks online at [...] 26 letters. [...] Photograph of the Fisher-Price letter set owned by a child who is now an adult synesthete with colors influenced by the toy. [...] have 10 or more matches to the magnet set in the empirical data. The probability of 10 or more matches to the magnet set for a ‘participant’ in the shuffled data was less than 0.009% across 5000 shuffles [...] though we stress that this is the source of the letter-color pairings rather than the cause of their synesthesia [...] This particular toy was only produced between 1971 and 1990
In one common form of synesthesia, known as grapheme–color synesthesia or color–graphemic synesthesia, letters or numbers are perceived as inherently colored.

gancho: Em 1967, um cientista fez uma roda girando parecer parada só cantarolando: o zumbido vibra os olhos nas órbitas e cria um efeito estroboscópico dentro do próprio olho.
explicacao: Tudo vem do efeito roda de carroça, a ilusão em que uma roda com raios parece girar mais devagar, ficar parada ou rodar para trás. Nos faroestes do cinema e da TV, a causa é o chamado aliasing temporal: a roda só é registrada em instantes separados. O mesmo ocorre sob luz que pisca. Em 1967, Rushton viu o efeito sob luz contínua enquanto cantarolava: o zumbido faz os olhos vibrarem nas órbitas, o que cria um efeito estroboscópico dentro do próprio olho. Cantarolando numa frequência múltipla da rotação, ele fez a roda parecer parada; um pouco acima ou abaixo, ela girava devagar para um lado ou para o outro. Há relatos de algo parecido com quem mastiga algo crocante, como cenoura, diante da TV: a imagem parece tremular, porque a mastigação vibraria os olhos num múltiplo da taxa de quadros. Mais estranho é que o efeito aparece até sob luz do sol, sem vibração nenhuma, como notou Schouten no mesmo ano. Uma hipótese diz que a visão funciona em quadros, como um filme; outra, que detectores de movimento no sentido contrário também disparam. Há evidências para as duas, mas o peso pende para a segunda.

fontes.trecho: The wagon-wheel effect (alternatively called stagecoach-wheel effect) is an optical illusion in which a spoked wheel appears to rotate differently from its true rotation. The wheel can appear to rotate more slowly than the true rotation, it can appear stationary, or it can appear to rotate in the opposite direction from the true rotation (reverse rotation effect). The wagon-wheel effect is most often seen in film or television depictions of stagecoaches or wagons in Western movies [...] In these recorded media, the effect is a result of temporal aliasing. It can also commonly be seen when a rotating wheel is illuminated by flickering light. [...] Stroboscopic conditions ensure that the visibility of a rotating wheel is broken into a series of very brief episodes, interrupted by episodes of invisibility. [...] Rushton (1967) observed the wagon-wheel effect under continuous illumination while humming. The humming vibrates the eyes in their sockets, effectively creating stroboscopic conditions within the eye. By humming at a frequency of a multiple of the rotation frequency, he was able to stop the rotation. By humming at slightly higher and lower frequencies, he was able to make the rotation reverse slowly and to make the rotation go slowly in the direction of rotation. A similar stroboscopic effect is now commonly observed by people eating crunchy foods, such as carrots, while watching TV: the image appears to shimmer. The crunching vibrates the eyes at a multiple of the frame rate of the TV. [...] The first to observe the wagon-wheel effect under truly continuous illumination (such as from the sun) was Schouten (1967). [...] There are two broad theories for the wagon-wheel effect under truly continuous illumination. The first is that human visual perception takes a series of still frames of the visual scene and that movement is perceived much like a movie. The second is Schouten's theory: that moving images are processed by visual detectors sensitive to the true motion and also by detectors sensitive to opposite motion from temporal aliasing. There is evidence for both theories, but the weight of evidence favours the latter.

gancho: Se uma imagem acompanhar cada movimento do olho e ficar sempre no mesmo ponto da retina, ela some em pouco tempo. A visão precisa de mudança: sem ela, até o que está bem à frente desaparece.
explicacao: Os cientistas conseguem fixar uma imagem na retina de três jeitos: com um projetor minúsculo preso a uma lente de contato, que se move junto com o olho; rastreando o olhar e deslocando a imagem para compensar cada movimento; ou com a pós-imagem de um flash forte, a mancha que fica depois de uma foto. Em todos os casos, o estímulo esmaece e some após pouco tempo. É a adaptação neural, um princípio geral dos sentidos: estímulos que não variam saem da consciência. Um papelzinho pousado no antebraço deixa de ser sentido, mas volta a ser notado se o braço se mexe. Sem aparelho nenhum, dá para ver uma versão disso, o desvanecimento de Troxler, descrito pelo médico suíço Ignaz Troxler em 1804: ao fixar o olhar num ponto, uma mancha fixa na visão periférica se apaga. O efeito é mais forte se ela for pequena, de pouco contraste, borrada ou distante do ponto fixado. Na periferia, os pequenos movimentos involuntários do olho não bastam para levar a imagem a células novas. Em 2006, um estudo mostrou que pelo menos parte desse apagamento acontece no cérebro, não nos olhos.

fontes.trecho: When one fixates on a particular point for even a short period of time, an unchanging stimulus away from the fixation point will fade away and disappear. [...] Troxler's fading was first identified by Swiss physician Ignaz Paul Vital Troxler in 1804, who was practicing in Vienna at the time. [...] Troxler's fading has been attributed to the adaptation of neurons vital for perceiving stimuli in the visual system. It is part of the general principle in sensory systems that unvarying stimuli soon disappear from our awareness. For example, if a small piece of paper is dropped on the inside of one's forearm, it is felt for a short period of time. Soon, however, the sensation fades away. [...] But if one jiggles one's arm up and down, giving varying stimulation, one will continue to feel the paper. [...] A similar "sensory fading", or filling-in, can be seen of a fixated stimulus when its retinal image is made stationary on the retina (a stabilized retinal image). [...] First, one can mount a tiny projector on a contact lens. The projector shines an image into the eye. As the eye moves, the contact lens moves with it, so the image is always projected onto the same part of the retina; Second, one can monitor eye movements and move the stimulus to cancel the eye movements; Third, one can induce an afterimage, usually by an intense, brief flash, such as when one is photographed using a photographic flash [...] In all these cases, the stimulus fades away after a short time and disappears. The Troxler effect is enhanced if the stimulus is small, is of low contrast (or "equiluminant"), or is blurred. The effect is enhanced the further the stimulus is away from the fixation point. [...] This means that the small, involuntary eye movements made when fixating on something fail to move the stimulus onto a new cell's receptive field, in effect giving unvarying stimulation. Hsieh and Tse showed in 2006 that at least some portion of the perceptual fading occurred in the brain, not in the eyes.

gancho: O mesmo rosto neutro de um ator, alternado com um prato de sopa, uma menina num caixão e uma mulher num divã, pareceu ao público mostrar fome, luto e desejo. Não se sabe se o filme do teste existiu.
explicacao: O experimento é atribuído ao cineasta russo Lev Kuleshov, nos anos 1910 e 1920. Ele teria montado trechos de filmes antigos, com o rosto inexpressivo do astro Ivan Mozzhukhin intercalado com aquelas imagens. Segundo o relato de Vsevolod Pudovkin, de 1929, a plateia elogiou a atuação: o ar pensativo diante da sopa, a tristeza diante da criança morta, a cobiça diante da mulher. Mas era sempre a mesma tomada. Kuleshov e Pudovkin contaram versões diferentes da história, e não se conhece filme ou foto que tenha sobrevivido. A ideia, porém, virou base da montagem soviética e foi explicada por Alfred Hitchcock em entrevistas. A ciência demorou a testá-la. Em 1992, uma recriação com 137 pessoas não achou o efeito, mas usava um único teste por participante, sujeito a ruído. Um estudo com ressonância magnética de 2006 e outro de 2016, com 36 participantes e 24 sequências, encontraram o efeito: um rosto neutro após uma cena triste parecia triste, e após uma cena alegre, alegre. Hoje os pesquisadores concordam que o contexto influencia de forma significativa a leitura de um rosto.

fontes.trecho: The Kuleshov effect (Russian: Эффект Кулешова) is a film editing (montage) effect demonstrated by Russian filmmaker Lev Kuleshov in the 1910s and 1920s. [...] When, where, and how Lev Kuleshov created this later cinematic research is not precisely known. He, like his collaborator Vsevolod Pudovkin, recounted differing versions, beginning soon after the work was done. No film or photo documentation is known to survive (if any edited film was ever created at all). Kuleshov edited a short film in which a shot of the expressionless face of Tsarist-era movie star Ivan Mozzhukhin (later known by the French name Ivan Mosjoukine) was alternated with various other shots (a bowl of soup, a girl in a coffin, a woman on a divan). The film was shown to an audience who believed that the expression on Mosjoukine's face was different each time he appeared, depending on whether he was "looking at" the bowl of soup, the girl in the coffin, or the woman on the divan, showing an expression of hunger, grief, or desire, respectively. The footage of Mosjoukine was actually the same shot each time. Vsevolod Pudovkin (who later claimed to have been the co-creator of the experiment) described in 1929 how the audience "raved about the acting [...] the heavy pensiveness of his mood over the forgotten soup, were touched and moved by the deep sorrow with which he looked on the dead child, and noted the lust with which he observed the woman. [...] The experiment itself was created by assembling fragments of pre-existing film from the Tsarist film industry, with no new material. [...] formed the theoretical basis of Soviet montage cinema [...] Alfred Hitchcock refers to the effect in his conversations with François Truffaut [...] The Kuleshov effect has been studied by psychologists only in recent years. Prince and Hensley (1992) recreated the original study design but did not find the alleged effect. The study had 137 participants but was a single-trial between-subject experiment, which is prone to noise in the data. Dean Mobbs et al. did a within-subject fMRI study in 2006 and found an effect for negative, positive, or neutral valence. When a neutral face was shown behind a sad scene, it seemed sad; when it was shown behind a happy scene, it seemed happy. In 2016, Daniel Barratt et al. tested 36 participants using 24 film sequences across five emotional conditions [...] researchers now agree that the context in which a face is shown has a significant effect on how the face is perceived.

gancho: Uma americana sem as duas amígdalas cerebrais não mostrou medo de cobras nem de filmes de terror. Mas, ao inalar ar com muito gás carbônico, entrou em pânico: ao que se sabe, seu primeiro medo desde a infância.
explicacao: Ela é conhecida na literatura científica como S.M. Nascida em 1965, tem a doença de Urbach-Wiethe, que destruiu as amígdalas dos dois lados do cérebro desde o fim da infância. Descrita por cientistas em 1994 e apelidada pela imprensa de "a mulher sem medo", ela reagiu com curiosidade, e não com pavor, a cobras, aranhas, uma casa mal-assombrada e trechos de filmes como O Iluminado. Na vida real, foi ameaçada com faca e com arma de fogo sem mostrar desespero, e não consegue reconhecer medo no rosto dos outros. Por isso a amígdala parecia indispensável para o medo. Num estudo posterior, pesquisadores esperavam que a lesão reduzisse o medo provocado pela inalação de ar com 35% de CO2, que dá sensação de sufocamento. Deu o contrário: S.M. e duas gêmeas idênticas com a mesma lesão tiveram ataques de pânico, enquanto só 3 de 12 voluntários sem lesão entraram em pânico. Pelo que os autores sabem, foi a primeira vez que S.M. sentiu medo desde a infância, e as três descreveram a sensação como totalmente nova. A conclusão foi que a amígdala não é necessária para o medo e o pânico, e que o medo disparado por dentro do corpo, como pela falta de ar, segue um caminho diferente do medo de ameaças externas.

fontes.trecho: S.M., sometimes referred to as SM-046, is an American woman with a peculiar type of brain damage that physiologically reduces her ability to feel fear. First described by scientists in 1994, she has had exclusive and complete bilateral amygdala destruction since late childhood as a consequence of Urbach–Wiethe disease. Dubbed by the media as the "woman with no fear" [...] An experiment with S.M. revealed no fear in response to exposure and handling of snakes and spiders (including tarantulas), a walk through a haunted attraction [...] or fear-inducing film clips (e.g., The Blair Witch Project, The Shining, and The Silence of the Lambs), eliciting instead only interest, curiosity, and excitement [...] She is greatly impaired in recognizing negative social cues, such as being incapable of recognizing fear in the facial expressions of other people [...] She has been held up at both knifepoint and gunpoint, was almost killed in a domestic violence incident, and has received explicit death threats on multiple occasions. Despite the life-threatening nature of many of these situations, S.M. did not exhibit any signs of desperation, urgency, or other behavioral responses that would normally accompany such incidents. [...] S.M. is white and was born in 1965.

fontes.titulo: Fear and panic in humans with bilateral amygdala damage (Feinstein et al., Nature Neuroscience, 2013)
fontes.trecho: Surprisingly, we found that inhalation of 35% CO2 evoked not only fear, but also panic attacks, in three rare patients with bilateral amygdala damage. These results indicate that the amygdala is not required for fear and panic, and make an important distinction between fear triggered by external threats from the environment versus fear triggered internally by CO2. [...] Inhaling CO2 stimulates breathing and can provoke both air hunger and fear [...] Therefore, we hypothesized that bilateral amygdala lesions would reduce CO2-evoked fear in humans. [...] In contrast to our prediction, patient SM reported fear in response to a 35% CO2 inhalation challenge. To our knowledge, this was the first time SM experienced fear in any setting, laboratory or otherwise, since childhood [...] we tested two additional patients (AM and BG), monozygotic twin sisters with focal bilateral amygdala lesions due to Urbach-Wiethe disease [...] By contrast, only 3 of 12 panicked in the matched, neurologically-intact comparison group [...] all patients found the feelings induced by the CO2 to be novel and described the experience as

gancho: A nostalgia já foi doença. O nome foi criado em 1688, numa tese de medicina, para o mal dos mercenários suíços longe de casa, e havia relatos de mortes. Certas canções da terra natal teriam sido proibidas a eles.
explicacao: O autor do termo foi Johannes Hofer, que o usou na sua dissertação em Basileia. Ele juntou duas palavras gregas: nóstos, a volta para casa, e algos, a dor. A condição também era chamada de "mal suíço", porque aparecia muito entre soldados suíços que, servindo longe de casa, definhavam de saudade das paisagens da terra natal. Entre os sintomas listados estavam desmaios, febre alta e até a morte. Casos fatais eram conhecidos, e alguns soldados foram curados do jeito mais simples: dispensados e mandados para casa. Mesmo assim, receber o diagnóstico era visto como um insulto. Segundo relatos da época, as canções suíças chamadas Ranz des vaches, ou Kuhreihen, eram proibidas aos mercenários, por despertarem a saudade a ponto de causar deserção, doença ou morte. Em 1767, o dicionário de música de Jean-Jacques Rousseau afirmou que os soldados eram ameaçados de punição severa se as cantassem. No século XVIII, houve cientistas que procuraram no corpo um "osso da nostalgia". Por volta de 1850, ela foi deixando de ser uma doença própria, embora ainda fosse diagnosticada em soldados na Guerra Civil americana. Hoje é vista como uma emoção agridoce e muitas vezes benéfica, ligada a melhora do humor e à sensação de conexão com os outros.

fontes.trecho: Nostalgia is an emotion which is often described as a bittersweet longing for the past [...] the word was coined by a 17th-century medical student to describe the anxieties displayed by Swiss mercenaries fighting away from home. [...] Nostalgia has been found to have important psychological functions, such as to improve mood, increase social connectedness [...] The term was coined in 1688 by Johannes Hofer (1669–1752) in his dissertation in Basel. The word nostalgia was compound of the ancient Greek words nóstos (return home) and algia (pain). Hofer introduced nostalgia or mal du pays, "homesickness", for the condition also known as mal du Suisse, "Swiss illness", because of its frequent occurrence in Swiss mercenaries who in the plains of Switzerland were pining for their landscapes. Symptoms were also thought to include fainting, high fever, and death. [...] Cases resulting in death were known and soldiers were sometimes successfully treated by being discharged and sent home. Receiving a diagnosis was, however, generally regarded as an insult. In the eighteenth century, scientists were looking for a locus of nostalgia, a nostalgic bone. By the 1850s, nostalgia was losing its status as a particular disease [...] Nostalgia was, however, still diagnosed among soldiers as late as the American Civil War. [...] Swiss nostalgia was linked to the singing of Ranz des vaches or Kuhreihen, which were forbidden to Swiss mercenaries because they led to nostalgia to the point of desertion, illness or death. The 1767 Dictionnaire de Musique by Jean-Jacques Rousseau claims that Swiss mercenaries were threatened with severe punishment to prevent them from singing their Swiss songs.

gancho: Em 1868, Darwin mostrou a visitas fotos de um velho cujo rosto era contraído por eletrodos e anotou, sem dar nenhuma pista, que emoção cada um via ali. Hoje isso se chamaria de teste cego.
explicacao: Darwin preparava o livro A expressão das emoções no homem e nos animais. As fotos eram do médico francês Duchenne, que aplicava correntes elétricas nos músculos do rosto para descobrir quais deles formavam cada expressão. O modelo principal era um homem idoso, magro e desdentado, cujas rugas marcavam bem cada contração, e que tinha uma condição médica que deixara o rosto quase sem sensibilidade. Darwin admirava o trabalho, mas duvidava que cada emoção tivesse músculos próprios. Entre março e novembro de 1868, mostrou as melhores imagens, sem uma palavra de explicação, a mais de vinte pessoas de várias idades e dos dois sexos, e registrou as respostas com as palavras delas, marcando em azul as que batiam com a descrição original e em vermelho as que não batiam. Não era um experimento no sentido moderno: não houve grupo de controle, e o primeiro grupo de visitas viu só sete das onze fotos. Em 2011 e 2012, o Darwin Correspondence Project refez o teste on-line com as mesmas imagens e recebeu mais de 18 mil respostas. Mais da metade reconheceu a surpresa, o terror e o pesar, mas as emoções mais complexas geraram respostas muito dispersas, como já tinha acontecido com os visitantes de Darwin.

fontes.trecho: Between March and November 1868, while Darwin was researching his book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, he showed a succession of visitors a set of photographs of human faces, some with the muscles artificially contracted by electric probes, and asked them what emotion they thought the photographs conveyed. [...] We collected over 18,000 (completely anonymous) responses between October 2011 and March 2012 [...] Duchenne had set out to find the muscles responsible for creating particular expressions [...] an old, toothless, man, with a thin face [...] His age and leanness meant that the contraction of his muscles produced particularly good wrinkles, but the old man had another advantage from Duchenne's point of view: he suffered from a medical condition that had left him with little feeling in his face. [...] Darwin was fascinated by the photographs, and admired Duchenne's achievements, but was sceptical of his claim to have identified individual muscles responsible for the expression of particular emotions. [...] It fortunately occurred to me to show several of the best plates, without a word of explanation, to above twenty educated persons of various ages and both sexes, asking them, in each case, by what emotion or feeling the old man was supposed to be agitated; and I recorded their answers in the words which they used. [...] Such an experiment would be described today as a "single-blind" test [...] the first batch of visitors saw only seven of the eventual set of eleven photographs [...] Darwin colour-coded the responses, marking those that agreed with the original description in blue crayon and those that didn't in red [...] Darwin's experiment was not a scientific experiment as we understand it today: there was no control group

fontes.titulo: Results of the Darwin Online Emotions Experiment (Darwin Correspondence Project)
fontes.trecho: For instance, over 50% identified photographs 2 (surprise), 3 (terror), 4 (grief and despair) with the correct or very similar emotion [...] However, for the perhaps more complex emotions depicted in photographs 5 to 11, hardly any of the participants identified the exact emotion and there was a greater range of, often conflicting, interpretations. This was true of Darwin's subjects as well.

gancho: Um clássico de 1988: quem segurava uma caneta nos dentes, forçando um sorriso sem perceber, achava os cartuns mais engraçados. Em 2016, 17 laboratórios refizeram o teste e não encontraram o efeito.
explicacao: O experimento testava a hipótese do feedback facial, que vem de ideias de Charles Darwin e William James: a expressão do rosto influenciaria a própria emoção. Fritz Strack e colegas pediram que voluntários vissem cartuns segurando uma caneta entre os dentes, o que puxa um sorriso, ou entre os lábios, o que impede o sorriso. O primeiro grupo deu notas maiores de graça. Como os participantes não sabiam que estavam sorrindo, o estudo virou prova de que o efeito não dependia de sugestão e entrou nas aulas de introdução à psicologia. Em 2016, uma replicação registrada em 17 laboratórios de vários países não achou efeito sistemático. Depois, outra equipe apontou uma diferença: na replicação, havia uma câmera filmando os participantes. Sem câmera, essa equipe voltou a obter o resultado original. Uma meta-análise de 2019 concluiu que o feedback facial existe, mas é pequeno. Depois, um consórcio internacional, a Many Smiles Collaboration, testou 3.878 pessoas em 19 países: imitar um rosto feliz ou mover de propósito os músculos do sorriso aumentou a sensação de felicidade, mas, com a caneta, o resultado foi inconclusivo. E, quando aparece, o efeito é pequeno. Sorrir parece mexer um pouco com o humor; quanto, e em que condições, ainda está em discussão.

fontes.trecho: The facial feedback hypothesis, rooted in the conjectures of Charles Darwin and William James, is that one's facial expression directly affects their emotional experience. [...] However, a 2019 meta-analysis, which generally confirmed small but significant effects [...] This was achieved by asking each participant to hold a pen in between their teeth (inducing a smile) or between their lips (inducing a frown) while instructed to view comedic cartoons. The study concluded that participants who engaged in a smiling expression (pen between teeth) reported a higher humor response to the cartoons as opposed to when participants held a frowning expression (pen between lips). This study proved to be highly influential in not only widespread acceptance of the facial feedback hypothesis (e.g., being commonly cited in introductory psychology classes) [...] In 2016, a large-scale Registered Replication Report was conducted with the purpose of meticulously replicating Strack, Martin, and Stepper's study and testing the facial feedback hypothesis across 17 different labs across varying countries and cultures. However, this study failed to reproduce the 1988 study's results [...] conducted in 17 labs did not find systematic effects of facial feedback. In a subsequent analysis, Noah et al. identified a significant methodological discrepancy (camera directed on participants) and replicated the original results under the no-camera condition.

fontes.titulo: A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration (Coles et al., Nature Human Behaviour)
fontes.trecho: Data from n = 3,878 participants spanning 19 countries indicated that a facial mimicry and voluntary facial action task could both amplify and initiate feelings of happiness. However, evidence of facial feedback effects was less conclusive when facial feedback was manipulated unobtrusively via a pen-in-mouth task. [...] Because participants in this pen-in-mouth study were presumably unaware they were smiling, the authors concluded that facial feedback effects were not driven by demand characteristics [...] facial feedback effects, when present, were small

gancho: Quando alguém faz cócegas em ratos, eles soltam chamados ultrassônicos apelidados de risada, dão pulos de alegria e correm atrás da mão. Se estiverem ansiosos, param de "rir".
explicacao: Em certas situações, ratos emitem chamados de 50 kHz, agudos demais para o ouvido humano. Esses chamados aumentam com coisas prazerosas, como brincar e acasalar, e diminuem diante de coisas desagradáveis. Por isso foi proposto que reflitam um estado parecido com a alegria humana mais primitiva, e eles ganharam o apelido de "risada". De tudo o que provoca esses chamados, as cócegas feitas por pessoas são o que mais os produz. Num estudo de 2016, Shimpei Ishiyama e Michael Brecht, da Universidade Humboldt de Berlim, viram que os ratos eram mais sensíveis na barriga e embaixo das patas, e que depois das cócegas davam saltos espontâneos de alegria, comportamento visto em vários mamíferos contentes. Também brincavam com a mão do pesquisador e a perseguiam, com chamados parecidos. No córtex somatossensorial, na região que representa o tronco, havia neurônios que disparavam forte com as cócegas, e respostas muito parecidas apareciam durante a brincadeira, mesmo sem toque. Estimular esses neurônios com eletricidade bastou para os ratos soltarem os chamados. Já deixar os animais ansiosos reduziu a atividade dessas células e calou os chamados. Brecht sugeriu que talvez as cócegas sejam um truque do cérebro para recompensar a interação e a brincadeira.

fontes.trecho: Research with rats has revealed that under particular conditions, they emit 50-kHz ultrasonic vocalisations (USV) which have been postulated to reflect a positive affective state (emotion) analogous to primitive human joy; these calls have been termed "laughter". The 50 kHz USVs in rats are uniquely elevated by hedonic stimuli—such as tickling, rewarding electrical brain stimulation, amphetamine injections, mating, play, and aggression—and are suppressed by aversive stimuli. Of all manipulations that elicit 50 kHz chirps in rats, tickling by humans elicits the highest rate of these calls.

fontes.titulo: Why are we ticklish? Rats are surprisingly ticklish when their mood is right (Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, via ScienceDaily, 2016)
fontes.trecho: Earlier work had shown that young rats respond with 50 kHz ultrasonic "laughter-calls" to tickling by humans. [...] As judged by their calls, rats were most ticklish on the belly and underneath their feet. Rats often performed unsolicited joy jumps after tickling, a behavior that can be seen in joyful subjects in various mammalian species. Rats also played with the researcher's hand and chased it, and emitted similar calls during play. [...] The researchers (Shimpei Ishiyama & Michael Brecht) [...] In the trunk region of the somatosensory cortex, the researchers observed nerve cells that responded strongly to tickling. Interestingly, the researchers found very similar brain responses during play behaviours as during tickling, even though the rats were not touched by the scientist. Making rats anxious -- which reduces ticklishness - also reduced the activity in these cells and suppressed the calls. Remarkably, rats emitted calls just to electric stimulation of the cells in the trunk region of the somatosensory cortex without being tickled. [...] Perhaps ticklishness is a trick of the brain that rewards interacting and playing. [...] November 11, 2016

gancho: Abelhas sacudidas por 60 segundos, como num ataque à colmeia, passam a ver o copo meio vazio: diante de um cheiro ambíguo, apostam mais que ele traz castigo. É o mesmo viés pessimista de cães e ratos estressados.
explicacao: O teste partiu de uma técnica usada em vertebrados. Primeiro, as abelhas aprenderam que uma mistura de dois odores anunciava água com açúcar, e outra, uma solução amarga de quinino ou uma recompensa menor. Elas mostravam a expectativa esticando ou recolhendo a probóscide, a "língua" do inseto. Logo depois do treino, metade foi sacudida com vigor por 60 segundos, para simular o ataque de um predador, como o texugo-do-mel, que arromba colmeias cavando. Em até 5 minutos, todas passaram a sentir cinco cheiros: os dois aprendidos e três misturas intermediárias. As abelhas sacudidas recolheram mais a probóscide diante do cheiro ruim e da mistura mais parecida com ele, como se esperassem o pior. Num outro grupo, a sacudida baixou os níveis de dopamina, octopamina e serotonina na hemolinfa, o "sangue" dos insetos. Esse viés de interpretar o ambíguo como ameaça acompanha a ansiedade em pessoas e já tinha aparecido em ratos, ovelhas, cães, estorninhos e pintinhos. Os autores não afirmam que as abelhas sentem algo. Mas argumentam que seria incoerente tratar esse viés como sinal de ansiedade em cães e ratos e negá-lo nas abelhas.

fontes.titulo: Agitated honeybees exhibit pessimistic cognitive biases (Bateson et al., Current Biology, 2011)
fontes.trecho: Here, we ask whether honeybees display a pessimistic cognitive bias when they are subjected to an anxiety-like state induced by vigorous shaking designed to simulate a predatory attack. We show for the first time that agitated bees are more likely to classify ambiguous stimuli as predicting punishment. Shaken bees also have lower levels of hemolymph dopamine, octopamine, and serotonin. [...] negative affective states such as anxiety are associated with increased expectation of punishment, greater attention to potential threats, and a tendency to interpret ambiguous stimuli as if they were threats [...] we trained honeybees to extend their mouthparts to a two-component odor mixture (CS+) predicting a reward (e.g., 1.00 or 2.00 [...] and to withhold their mouthparts from another mixture (CS [...] predicting either punishment or a less valuable reward (e.g., 0.01 [...] quinine solution or 0.3 [...] Immediately after training, half of the honeybees were subjected to vigorous shaking for 60 [...] to simulate the state produced by a predatory attack on a concealed colony. [...] brood predators and honey thieves such as the honey badger (Mellivora capensis) have been observed to use their accomplished digging skills to break into beehives. [...] Within 5 [...] of the shaking manipulation, all of the trained bees began a sequence of unreinforced test trials with five odor stimuli presented in a randomly chosen order for each bee: the CS+, the CS [...] and three novel odors composed of ratios intermediate between the two learned mixtures. Shaken honeybees were more likely to withhold their mouthparts from the CS [...] and from the most similar novel odor [...] Our results add an invertebrate animal to the growing list of vertebrates, including rats, sheep, dogs, starlings, and domestic chicks, that when subjected to various forms of negative, stressful manipulations exhibit pessimistic judgment biases. [...] Although our results do not allow us to make any claims about the presence of negative subjective feelings in honeybees, they call into question how we identify emotions in any nonhuman animal. It is logically inconsistent to claim that the presence of pessimistic cognitive biases should be taken as confirmation that dogs or rats are anxious but to deny the same conclusion in the case of honeybees.

Immediately after training, half of the honeybees were subjected to vigorous shaking for 60 s to simulate the state produced by a predatory attack on a concealed colony. This shaking reduced levels of octopamine, dopamine, and serotonin in the hemolymph of a separate group of honeybees

gancho: Lagostins estressados com choques passam a se esconder nas partes escuras de um labirinto, num comportamento parecido com ansiedade. Uma injeção de um ansiolítico usado em pessoas os faz voltar a explorar.
explicacao: Lagostins costumam explorar lugares novos, mas têm uma preferência geral pelo escuro. No estudo, publicado na Science em 2014 por pesquisadores do CNRS e da Universidade de Bordeaux, os animais da espécie Procambarus clarkii foram expostos repetidamente a um campo elétrico durante trinta minutos. Depois foram postos num labirinto em forma de cruz, debaixo d'água, com dois braços iluminados, que os repelem, e dois escuros. Os estressados ficaram nas áreas escuras, enquanto os do grupo de controle percorreram o labirinto inteiro, e esse estado se dissipou em cerca de uma hora. Os lagostins estressados tinham mais serotonina no cérebro e mais glicose no sangue, sinal de resposta ao estresse. Quando receberam clordiazepóxido, um benzodiazepínico usado para tratar ansiedade em humanos, eles se acalmaram e voltaram a entrar nas áreas claras. Um estudo seguinte, com a mesma espécie, mostrou que a intensidade desse comportamento crescia com a intensidade do choque até se estabilizar, uma relação comum na ansiedade de vertebrados. Para os autores, a evitação causada pelo estresse nos lagostins tem semelhanças marcantes com a ansiedade dos vertebrados, sinal de que esses mecanismos surgiram cedo na evolução e foram preservados.

fontes.trecho: Crayfish naturally explore new environments but display a general preference for dark places. A 2014 study on the freshwater crayfish Procambarus clarkii tested their responses in a fear paradigm [...] Furthermore, shocked crayfish had relatively higher brain serotonin concentrations coupled with elevated blood glucose, which indicates a stress response. Moreover, the crayfish calmed down when they were injected with the benzodiazepine anxiolytic, chlordiazepoxide, used to treat anxiety in humans, and they entered the dark as normal. The authors of the study concluded "[...] stress-induced avoidance behavior in crayfish exhibits striking homologies with vertebrate anxiety." A follow-up study using the same species confirmed the anxiolytic effect of chlordiazepoxide, but moreover, the intensity of the anxiety-like behaviour was dependent on the intensity of the electric shock until reaching a plateau. Such a quantitative relationship between stress and anxiety is also a very common feature of human and vertebrate anxiety.

fontes.titulo: Anxiety-like behavior in invertebrates opens research avenues (CNRS, via ScienceDaily, 2014)
fontes.trecho: CNRS researchers and the Université de Bordeaux have produced and observed anxiety-like behavior in crayfish, which disappears when a dose of anxiolytic is injected. This work, published in Science on June 13, 2014, shows that the neuronal mechanisms related to anxiety have been preserved throughout evolution. [...] repeatedly exposed crayfish to an electric field for thirty minutes. They then placed the crayfish in an aquatic cross-shaped maze. Two arms of the maze were lit up (which repels the crustaceans) and two were dark-which they find reassuring. [...] Those made anxious tended to remain in the dark areas of the maze, by contrast to control crayfish, which explored the entire maze. [...] This emotional state wore itself out after about one hour. [...] This shows how early neural mechanisms that trigger or inhibit anxiety-like behavior appeared in the evolutionary process and that they have been well preserved over time.

gancho: O rosto de olhos arregalados e boca aberta, que no Ocidente se lê como medo, foi lido como raiva e ameaça por jovens das ilhas Trobriand, na Papua-Nova Guiné. Lá, objetos do século XIX já o retratavam como ameaça.
explicacao: Cientistas, Darwin entre eles, investigam há muito tempo se todos os humanos têm as mesmas emoções básicas, e a linha de pesquisa dominante sustentava que as expressões faciais são entendidas em toda parte. Mas a suposição se baseava sobretudo em sociedades ocidentais. Num estudo publicado em 2016, uma equipe da Boston College, da Universidade Autônoma de Madri e do Museu Americano de História Natural foi às ilhas Trobriand, cujos moradores relataram quase nenhum contato com antropólogos, turistas ocidentais ou gente da ilha principal. O antropólogo Sergio Jarillo passou 21 meses em campo e ensinou a língua local, o kilivila, ao psicólogo Carlos Crivelli, que ficou outros sete meses. Adolescentes trobriandeses atribuíram emoções e intenções a fotos de rostos e concordaram entre si bem menos do que amostras ocidentais. O rosto ofegante, tido no Ocidente como medo e submissão, foi ligado de forma consistente a raiva e ameaça. Quando se pediu que escolhessem o rosto ameaçador, os trobriandeses apontaram esse, e os espanhóis, um rosto carrancudo. Objetos da cultura local, com registros desde o século XIX, já retratavam essa cara como exibição de ameaça. O resultado não encerra o debate sobre emoções universais, mas mostra que a leitura de um rosto pode depender da cultura.

fontes.titulo: The fear gasping face as a threat display in a Melanesian society (Crivelli et al., PNAS, 2016), resumo no PubMed
fontes.trecho: The assumption that such interpretations are pancultural derives largely from Western societies. [...] In study 1, Trobriand adolescents were asked to attribute emotions, social motives, or both to a set of facial displays. Trobrianders showed a mixed and variable attribution pattern, although with much lower agreement than studies of Western samples. Remarkably, the gasping face (traditionally considered a display of fear and submission in the West) was consistently matched to two unpredicted categories: anger and threat. In study 2, adolescents were asked to select the face that was threatening; Trobrianders chose the

Published on October 19, 2016 [...] The Trobrianders chose the gasping face, while the subjects in Spain chose a scowling face categorized as [...] The findings from researchers at Boston College, Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, and the American Museum of Natural History [...] Scientists, including Charles Darwin, have been trying to determine whether or not all humans experience the same basic emotions. The leading research to date has held that facial expressions – and the emotions they represent – are universally understood. [...] Artifacts dating back to the 19th century show the Trobrianders’ own material culture has portrayed the gasping face – known in the local dialect as ekapunipuni matala migila – as an iconic threat display [...] The study participants reported nearly nonexistent contact with anthropologists, Western tourists, and residents from the Papua New Guinea mainland. [...] Sergio Jarillo, a social anthropologist, embedded himself in the islands for 21 months of fieldwork, eschewing the need for translators or guides. He worked closely with Carlos Crivelli, an experimental psychologist, to teach him the Kilivila language, which is the Trobriand vernacular, prior to Crivelli spending seven months doing fieldwork in the islands

gancho: Na síndrome de Capgras, a pessoa reconhece o rosto do marido ou da mãe, mas jura que é um impostor idêntico. Uma explicação: o rosto é reconhecido, mas a emoção que deveria vir junto não chega.
explicacao: O quadro foi descrito em 1923 pelo psiquiatra francês Joseph Capgras e por Jean Reboul-Lachaux. A paciente, apelidada de "Madame Macabre", dizia que sósias tinham tomado o lugar do marido e de outras pessoas que ela conhecia, e eles chamaram o fenômeno de "ilusão dos sósias". Uma pista para explicá-lo veio da prosopagnosia, a incapacidade de reconhecer rostos. Em 1984, um estudo mostrou que esses pacientes, embora não reconhecessem conscientemente rostos conhecidos, ainda reagiam a eles com uma resposta automática do corpo, medida pela condutância da pele. Em 1990, os psicólogos Hadyn Ellis e Andy Young propuseram que Capgras seria a imagem no espelho disso: o reconhecimento consciente funciona, mas falha o sistema que gera a reação emocional automática diante de quem é familiar. A pessoa reconhece o rosto, sente que algo não está certo e conclui que é um impostor. Só a falta da reação emocional, porém, não basta: o mesmo padrão já foi visto em pessoas sem delírio, e por isso se propõe um segundo fator, uma falha no raciocínio que transforma a estranheza em crença. Em 1997, um estudo com cinco pacientes com Capgras confirmou que eles reconheciam os rostos, mas não tinham a reação automática normal, e respondiam a conhecidos como respondiam a estranhos. O quadro aparece em psicoses, como a esquizofrenia, em lesões cerebrais e em demências.

fontes.trecho: Capgras delusion or Capgras syndrome (CS) is a psychiatric disorder in which a person holds a delusion that a friend, spouse, parent, other close family member, or pet has been replaced by an identical impostor. [...] The delusion most commonly occurs in individuals diagnosed with a psychotic disorder, usually schizophrenia; it has also been seen in brain injury, dementia with Lewy bodies, and other forms of dementia. [...] Capgras syndrome is named after Joseph Capgras, a French psychiatrist who first described the disorder in 1923 in his paper co-authored by Jean Reboul-Lachaux. They described the case of a French woman, "Madame Macabre", who complained that corresponding "doubles" had taken the places of her husband and other people she knew. Capgras and Reboul-Lachaux first called the syndrome "l'illusion des sosies" [...] In this condition, patients are unable to recognize faces consciously, despite being able to recognize other types of visual objects. However, a 1984 study by Bauer showed that even though conscious face recognition was impaired, patients with the condition showed autonomic arousal (measured by a galvanic skin response measure) to familiar faces [...] In a 1990 paper published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, psychologists Hadyn Ellis and Andy Young hypothesized that patients with Capgras delusion may have a "mirror image" or double dissociation of prosopagnosia, in that their conscious ability to recognize faces was intact, but they might have damage to the system which produces the automatic emotional arousal to familiar faces. This might lead to the experience of recognizing someone while feeling something was not "quite right" about them. In 1997, Ellis and his colleagues published a study of five patients with Capgras delusion (all diagnosed with schizophrenia) and confirmed that although they could consciously recognize the faces, they did not show the normal automatic emotional arousal response. The same low level of autonomic response was shown in the presence of strangers. [...] Most likely, more than a mere impairment of the automatic emotional arousal response is necessary to form the Capgras delusion, as the same pattern has been reported in patients showing no signs of delusions.

gancho: Até o século XIX, filósofos e médicos não falavam em "emoções" como uma categoria: dividiam a vida afetiva em paixões, afetos e sentimentos. Os primeiros livros sobre "as emoções" saíram entre as décadas de 1830 e 1850.
explicacao: A palavra é antiga. Em francês, "émotion" foi usada em 1543 pelo humanista Étienne Dolet, numa tradução de Cícero, e designava uma perturbação física. O que é recente é a ideia de juntar raiva, medo, amor e tristeza num só grupo de estados mentais a ser estudado. Por muitos séculos, o pensamento moral se apoiou numa divisão feita pelos teólogos Agostinho e Tomás de Aquino. De um lado estavam as paixões, movimentos violentos que podiam levar ao pecado. Do outro, os afetos mais virtuosos, como o amor e a compaixão, que cabia cultivar. Segundo o historiador Thomas Dixon, "emoção" só virou um termo teórico pleno no século XIX, sobretudo pela influência de dois filósofos e médicos escoceses, Thomas Brown e Charles Bell. A troca não foi imediata: em 1836, o polímata inglês William Whewell comentou que a proposta de chamar os desejos e afetos de "as Emoções" ainda não tinha sido aceita, e em 1862 ele continuava preferindo a expressão antiga. Mais tarde, William James publicou o artigo "O que é uma emoção?". Para Dixon, um século e um quarto depois, ainda há pouco consenso científico sobre a resposta.

fontes.titulo: "Emotion": The history of a keyword in crisis (Thomas Dixon, Emotion Review, 2012)
fontes.trecho: has named a psychological category and a subject for systematic enquiry only since the 19th century. [...] originating as a translation of the French [...] motion, meaning a physical disturbance. [...] becoming a fully fledged theoretical term in the following century, especially through the influence of two Scottish philosopher-physicians, Thomas Brown and Charles Bell. [...] In that year William James wrote an influential article in Mind entitled [...] A century and a quarter later, however, there seems to be little scientific consensus on the answer to his question [...] The first books written on the subject of [...] appeared between the 1830s and 1850s. [...] In 1836 the English polymath William Whewell commented that the proposal to refer to what he called [...] of human nature as [...] had not been generally accepted. Even as late as 1862, Whewell was expressing his preference for the compound phrase [...] The passions were indeed violent forces that could conflict with reason and lead an individual into sin. [...] that the good Christian should avoid, and those more virtuous and Godly affections of love and compassion to which they might rightly aspire. [...] undergirded moral-philosophical thought for many centuries.

The word emotion, which comes from Latin and means "a movement of something from the inside towards the outside", was coined in 1543 by the French humanist Étienne Dolet (1509-1546), who employed it in French (emotion) in his translation of Cicero's Tusculanae Disputationes.

gancho: Um choque emocional pode enfraquecer o coração de repente, imitando um infarto: é a síndrome do coração partido. Mas, num registro internacional, 4,1% dos casos com gatilho emocional vieram de uma alegria.
explicacao: O nome médico é síndrome de takotsubo: um enfraquecimento súbito e temporário do músculo do coração, em geral depois de um estresse físico ou emocional forte. Foi batizada em 1990 pelo médico japonês Hikaru Sato, porque o ventrículo esquerdo fica com o formato de um takotsubo, o pote usado no Japão para pegar polvos. O quadro costuma imitar um infarto, com dor no peito e alterações no eletrocardiograma. O mecanismo não é bem entendido, mas suspeita-se de uma descarga maciça de hormônios do estresse, como a adrenalina. Como o gatilho costuma ser luto, raiva ou medo, ganhou o apelido popular. Um estudo do Registro Internacional de Takotsubo examinou 1.750 pacientes e achou 485 com um gatilho emocional claro. Em 20 deles, o evento tinha sido feliz: uma festa de aniversário, o casamento de um filho, um reencontro com colegas de escola depois de 50 anos, tornar-se avó, a vitória do time de rúgbi favorito. Os pesquisadores chamaram esses casos de "síndrome do coração feliz". Os sintomas foram praticamente os mesmos dos casos tristes, como dor no peito em cerca de nove de cada dez pacientes dos dois grupos. Nos dois grupos, quase todos os pacientes eram mulheres.

fontes.titulo: Happy heart syndrome: role of positive emotional stress in takotsubo syndrome (Ghadri et al., European Heart Journal, 2016)
fontes.trecho: Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) is typically provoked by negative stressors such as grief, anger, or fear leading to the popular term [...] Of 1750 TTS patients, we identified a total of 485 with a definite emotional trigger. Of these, 4.1% (n = 20) presented with pleasant preceding events [...] including symptoms such as chest pain [89.5% (17/19) vs. 90.2% (412/457), P = 1.0]. [...] Birthday party [...] Son's wedding [...] Meeting after 50 years with friends from high school [...] Becoming grandmother [...] Favourite rugby team won game [...] Women were over-represented (P < 0.001) without differences between both groups
