Our second experiment was aimed at manipulating the beliefs of the experimenters: Half were led to think that participants would walk slower when primed congruently, and the other half was led to expect the opposite. Strikingly, we obtained a walking speed effect, but only when experimenters believed participants would indeed walk slower. This suggests that both priming and experimenters' expectations are instrumental in explaining the walking speed effect. Further, debriefing was suggestive of awareness of the primes. [...] Second, walking speed was measured using a manual stopwatch — a method that is prone to error and bias. [...] took place in an empty hallway located on a vacant floor of a Université Libre de Bruxelles building. [...] Two infrared sensors were hidden in the hallway [...] we also asked the experimenters to measure participants' walking time using a manual stopwatch [...] as the primed participants did not walk faster when tested by an experimenter who believed they would walk faster.

In the early 2010s, two direct replication attempts failed to reproduce results from social psychologist John Bargh's much-cited "elderly-walking" study (originally published in 1996). This experiment was part of a series of three studies that had been widely cited throughout the years, was regularly taught in university courses

gancho: Em experimentos de 1967, cães que levavam choques inescapáveis desistiam de fugir até quando podiam: teriam aprendido que nada adiantava. Em 2016, os dois criadores da teoria escreveram que ela estava ao contrário.
explicacao: Martin Seligman começou a pesquisa em 1967, na Universidade da Pensilvânia. Num dos primeiros experimentos, cães presos a arreios levavam choques. Uns podiam desligá-los apertando uma alavanca; outros, ligados a esses, recebiam choques iguais, mas sua alavanca não fazia nada. Depois, numa caixa em que bastava pular uma barreira baixa para escapar, os primeiros aprendiam logo, e a maioria dos outros se deitava e gania. Para "curá-los", os pesquisadores precisaram mover as patas dos cães pelo caminho da fuga pelo menos duas vezes; ameaças, recompensas e demonstrações não funcionaram. A explicação, de Seligman e Maier, era que os animais aprendiam que suas ações não importavam. Em 2016, num artigo de revisão, Maier e Seligman afirmaram que o mecanismo, hoje bem mapeado na biologia, mostra o oposto: a passividade diante de um sofrimento prolongado não é aprendida. É a reação padrão, comandada pela atividade da serotonina no núcleo dorsal da rafe, que inibe a fuga. O que se aprende é o controle: quando o animal detecta que pode agir, o córtex pré-frontal medial freia aquele núcleo. Os autores especulam que isso pode ter implicações importantes para o tratamento da depressão.

fontes.trecho: American psychologist Martin Seligman initiated research on learned helplessness in 1967 at the University of Pennsylvania as an extension of his interest in depression. [...] In Part 1 of this study, three groups of dogs were placed in harnesses. [...] Dogs in Group 2 were given electric shocks at random times, which the dog could end by pressing a lever. Each dog in Group 3 was paired with a Group 2 dog; whenever a Group 2 dog got a shock, its paired dog in Group 3 got a shock of the same intensity and duration, but its lever did not stop the shock. [...] All of the dogs could escape shocks on one side of the box by jumping over a low partition to the other side. The dogs in Groups 1 and 2 quickly learned this task and escaped the shock. Most of the Group 3 dogs‍—‍which had previously learned that nothing they did had any effect on shocks‍—‍simply lay down passively and whined when they were shocked. [...] To change this expectation, experimenters physically picked up the dogs and moved their legs, replicating the actions the dogs would need to take in order to escape from the electrified grid. This had to be done at least twice before the dogs would start willfully jumping over the barrier on their own. In contrast, threats, rewards, and observed demonstrations had no effect on the "helpless" Group 3 dogs.

fontes.titulo: Learned helplessness at fifty: Insights from neuroscience (Maier e Seligman, Psychological Review, 2016)
fontes.trecho: Learned helplessness at fifty: Insights from neuroscience. [...] Maier SF, Seligman ME. [...] Seligman and Maier (1967) theorized that animals learned that outcomes were independent of their responses-that nothing they did mattered-and that this learning undermined trying to escape. The mechanism of learned helplessness is now very well-charted biologically, and the original theory got it backward. Passivity in response to shock is not learned. It is the default, unlearned response to prolonged aversive events and it is mediated by the serotonergic activity of the dorsal raphe nucleus, which in turn inhibits escape. This passivity can be overcome by learning control, with the activity of the medial prefrontal cortex, which subserves the detection of control leading to the automatic inhibition of the dorsal raphe nucleus. [...] We speculate that default passivity and the compensating detection and expectation of control may have substantial implications for how to treat depression. [...] "pubYear":"2016"

gancho: Pelas normas de 1997, os americanos testados em 1932 teriam QI médio de 80, e quase um quarto pareceria "deficiente". As notas de QI subiram uns três pontos por década. Se a inteligência subiu junto, é outra história.
explicacao: Os testes de QI são recalibrados de tempos em tempos: a média de uma amostra nova de pessoas vira o novo 100. Quando gente de gerações mais recentes responde às versões antigas, a média dela fica quase sempre bem acima de 100. Nos Estados Unidos, o ganho foi de uns três pontos por década nas escalas Wechsler, e um estudo publicado em 2009 viu a nota de crianças britânicas nas Matrizes de Raven subir 14 pontos entre 1942 e 2008. O fenômeno leva o nome de James Flynn, que fez muito para documentá-lo, mas quem cunhou o termo foram os autores do livro "The Bell Curve", de 1994. Uma explicação proposta pelo próprio Flynn: a vida moderna, com trabalho mais exigente, mais tecnologia e famílias menores, acostumou muito mais gente a manipular abstrações, como hipóteses e categorias, que ocupam boa parte dos testes. O exemplo dele é a pergunta "o que um cachorro e um coelho têm em comum?". Hoje, a resposta típica é que os dois são mamíferos. Há um século, alguém poderia responder que se caça coelho com cachorro. O psicólogo Ulric Neisser resumiu a dúvida: as notas sobem no mundo todo, mas se a inteligência em si subiu continua controverso.

fontes.trecho: When IQ tests are revised, they are again standardized using a new sample of test-takers, usually born more recently than the first; the average result is set to 100. When the new test subjects take the older tests, in almost every case their average scores are significantly above 100. [...] a study published in the year 2009 found that British children's average scores on the Raven's Progressive Matrices test rose by 14 IQ points from 1942 to 2008. [...] The Flynn effect is named for James Robert Flynn, who did much to document it and promote awareness of its implications. The term was coined by Richard Herrnstein and Charles Murray in their 1994 book The Bell Curve. [...] The average rate of increase seems to be about three IQ points per decade in the United States, as scaled by the Wechsler tests. [...] Ulric Neisser estimated that using the IQ values of 1997, the average IQ of the United States in 1932, according to the first Stanford–Binet Intelligence Scales standardization sample, was 80. Neisser states that "Hardly any of them would have scored 'very superior', but nearly one-quarter would have appeared to be 'deficient.'" He also wrote that "Test scores are certainly going up all over the world, but whether intelligence itself has risen remains controversial." [...] Environmental changes resulting from modernization—such as more intellectually demanding work, greater use of technology, and smaller families—have meant that a much larger proportion of people are more accustomed to manipulating abstract concepts such as hypotheses and categories than a century ago. Substantial portions of IQ tests deal with these abilities. Flynn gives, as an example, the question 'What do a dog and a rabbit have in common?' A modern respondent might say they are both mammals (an abstract, or a priori answer, which depends only on the meanings of the words dog and rabbit), whereas someone a century ago might have said that humans catch rabbits with dogs

gancho: Na Noruega, o QI médio dos recrutas subiu por décadas, virou e passou a cair. A virada aparece até comparando irmãos da mesma família, o que aponta o ambiente, e não os genes, como causa provável.
explicacao: No século XX, as notas em testes de inteligência subiram em boa parte do mundo, o chamado efeito Flynn. Nos últimos anos, porém, vários países viram o ritmo diminuir ou se inverter. Para separar as muitas explicações propostas, dois pesquisadores do Centro Ragnar Frisch, em Oslo, usaram registros oficiais e as notas dos testes cognitivos do alistamento militar de noruegueses nascidos entre 1962 e 1991. Como só os homens passavam pelo alistamento, só havia QI medido para eles. O estudo, publicado em 2018 na revista PNAS, mostrou que a subida, o ponto de virada e a queda posterior aparecem inteiros dentro das famílias, quando se comparam irmãos. Isso importa porque várias hipóteses para a queda envolvem genes ou fatores de ambiente que variam de uma família para outra, mas não entre irmãos. Comparando irmãos, o estudo não achou indício a favor delas, e a conclusão foi que fatores ambientais eram a causa provável. Outros pesquisadores lembram que parte da aparente reversão pode vir de mudanças culturais que deixam trechos dos testes desatualizados, e meta-análises de meados dos anos 2010 indicavam que, no conjunto, o efeito Flynn continuava, ainda que mais lento nos países desenvolvidos.

fontes.titulo: Flynn effect and its reversal are both environmentally caused (PNAS, 2018, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Flynn effect and its reversal are both environmentally caused. [...] Ragnar Frisch Centre for Economic Research, 0349 Oslo, Norway. [...] Population intelligence quotients increased throughout the 20th century-a phenomenon known as the Flynn effect-although recent years have seen a slowdown or reversal of this trend in several countries. To distinguish between the large set of proposed explanations, we categorize hypothesized causal factors by whether they accommodate the existence of within-family Flynn effects. Using administrative register data and cognitive ability scores from military conscription data covering three decades of Norwegian birth cohorts (1962-1991), we show that the observed Flynn effect, its turning point, and subsequent decline can all be fully recovered from within-family variation. The analysis controls for all factors shared by siblings and finds no evidence for prominent causal hypotheses of the decline implicating genes and environmental factors that vary between, but not within, families.

Some researchers have suggested the possibility of a mild reversal in the Flynn effect (i.e., a decline in IQ scores) in developed countries, beginning in the 1990s, sometimes referred to as reverse Flynn effect. In certain cases, this apparent reversal may be due to cultural changes rendering parts of intelligence tests obsolete. However, as of the mid-2010s, meta-analyses indicated that, overall, the Flynn effect continued, either at the same rate, or at a slower rate in developed countries. [...] Bratsberg & Rogeberg (2018) present evidence that the Flynn effect in Norway has reversed between the years 1962–1991, and that both the original rise in mean IQ scores and their subsequent decline within this period can be observed within families consisting of native-born parents and their children, indicating that environmental factors were the likely cause for these changes. Because IQ data was only available for male Norwegians, who were subject to military conscription

gancho: O sal iodado chegou aos EUA em 1924. Segundo um estudo, isso elevou o QI em cerca de um desvio-padrão no quarto da população com mais falta de iodo. Mas também houve um grande aumento de mortes ligadas à tireoide.
explicacao: A falta de iodo é a principal causa evitável de deficiência intelectual no mundo. Ela era comum até em países ricos antes do sal iodado, nos anos 1920, e depende de quanto iodo existe no solo e na água de cada lugar. Nos Estados Unidos, o bócio era muito frequente em volta dos Grandes Lagos e no noroeste do país. Um professor de pediatria da Universidade de Michigan, David Murray Cowie, levou o país a copiar a prática suíça de pôr iodeto no sal de cozinha. Em 1º de maio de 1924, o sal iodado começou a ser vendido em Michigan e, no outono, a Morton já o distribuía no país inteiro. Como a mudança foi rápida e a falta de iodo variava de região para região, três pesquisadores compararam os dados militares das duas guerras mundiais de quem nasceu antes e depois do sal iodado, em lugares pobres e ricos em iodo. No quarto da população mais carente, o QI subiu cerca de um desvio-padrão, o que, segundo eles, explicaria mais ou menos uma década da subida do QI americano, o efeito Flynn. O mesmo trabalho, publicado em 2017, registrou o lado ruim: um grande aumento de mortes ligadas à tireoide depois da adoção nacional, sobretudo de pessoas mais velhas em regiões onde a falta de iodo era comum.

fontes.titulo: The Cognitive Effects of Micronutrient Deficiency: Evidence from Salt Iodization in the United States (NBER)
fontes.trecho: Iodine deficiency is the leading cause of preventable mental retardation in the world today. The condition, which was common in the developed world until the introduction of iodized salt in the 1920s, is connected to low iodine levels in the soil and water. We examine the impact of salt iodization on cognitive outcomes in the US by taking advantage of this natural geographic variation. Salt was iodized over a very short period of time beginning in 1924. We use military data collected during WWI and WWII to compare outcomes of cohorts born before and after iodization, in localities that were naturally poor and rich in iodine. [...] find that for the one quarter of the population most deficient in iodine this intervention raised IQ by approximately one standard deviation. Our results can explain roughly one decade's worth of the upward [...] We also document a large increase in thyroid related deaths following the countrywide adoption of iodized salt, which affected mostly older individuals in localities with high prevalence of iodine deficiency. [...] Journal of the European Economic Association, vol 15(2), pages 355-387

In the early 20th century, goiters were especially prevalent in the region around the Great Lakes and the Pacific Northwest. David Murray Cowie, a professor of paediatrics at the University of Michigan, led the United States to adopt the Swiss practice of adding sodium iodide or potassium iodide to table and cooking salt. On May 1, 1924, iodized salt was sold commercially in Michigan. By the fall of 1924, Morton Salt Company began distributing iodized salt nationally. A 2017 study found that introducing iodized salt in 1924 raised the IQ of one-quarter of the population most deficient in iodine.

gancho: Binet criou o teste de inteligência para achar crianças francesas que precisavam de ajuda na escola, e via a inteligência como maleável. Nos EUA, um defensor da eugenia o traduziu e o levou para a triagem de imigrantes.
explicacao: Em 1904, o Ministério da Educação da França criou uma comissão para decidir se crianças com dificuldade de aprendizagem deviam ir para uma escola especial. Alfred Binet e o psiquiatra Théodore Simon montaram então testes para distinguir quem precisava de ajuda e quem podia seguir no ensino regular. A primeira versão saiu em 1905, e a completa, em 1908. Os dois insistiam que o desenvolvimento intelectual tinha ritmos variados e sofria influência do ambiente: a inteligência não dependia só da genética e não era fixa. Nos Estados Unidos, o teste mudou de função. Henry Goddard, defensor da eugenia, o traduziu para o inglês, distribuiu cerca de 22 mil cópias e introduziu o uso clínico da palavra "moron", para adultos com idade mental entre oito e doze anos. Em 1913, montou um programa de testes na ilha de Ellis para identificar entre os imigrantes os "débeis mentais" que escapavam ao olho dos fiscais de imigração. Num grupo pequeno de imigrantes judeus, húngaros, italianos e russos, cerca de 80% foram classificados assim. Desconfiado de números tão extremos, Goddard ajustou o critério, e a fatia caiu para uns 40%. Depois, Lewis Terman adaptou a escala em Stanford, e o nome de Simon praticamente sumiu da história do teste.

fontes.trecho: In 1904, Binet took part in a commission set up by the French Ministry of Education to decide whether school children with learning difficulties should be sent to a special boarding school [...] Simon, who was a young psychiatrist working in an asylum for children with intellectual deficiency. [...] Binet and Simon worked closely to develop more tests and questions that would distinguish between children who did and did not need help in attending regular education. In 1905 they published a preliminary version of their test for measuring intelligence [...] The full version of the test with age-appropriate standards was published in 1908 [...] They also stressed that intellectual development progressed at variable rates and could be influenced by the environment; therefore, intelligence was not based solely on genetics, was malleable rather than fixed [...] In 1908, H.H. Goddard, a champion of the eugenics movement, found utility in mental testing as a way to evidence the superiority of the white race. After studying abroad, Goddard brought the Binet-Simon Scale to the United States and translated it into English. Following Goddard in the U.S. mental testing movement was Lewis Terman, who took the Simon-Binet Scale and standardized it using a large American sample. [...] The name of Simon was all but erased from the record

for translating the Binet-Simon Intelligence Test into English in 1908 and distributing an estimated 22,000 copies of the translated test across the United States. He also introduced the term "moron" for clinical use. [...] A moron, by his definition, was any adult with a mental age between eight and twelve. [...] Goddard established an intelligence testing program on Ellis Island in 1913. The purpose of the program was to identify "feeble-minded" persons whose nature was not obvious to the subjective judgement of immigration officers [...] Goddard and his associates tested a group of 35 Jewish, 22 Hungarian, 50 Italian, and 45 Russian immigrants who had been identified as "representative of their respective groups". The results found that 83% of Jews, 80% of Hungarians, 79% of Italians, and 80% of Russians of the study population were "feeble-minded". [...] Not trusting such extreme results, Goddard then adjusted the threshold of "feeble-mindedness" such that only about 40% of the immigrants were deemed to be morons.

gancho: Em 1921, um estudo famoso selecionou crianças de QI altíssimo para acompanhar pela vida. Dois meninos testados e recusados, William Shockley e Luis Alvarez, ganharam o Nobel de Física. Nenhum dos escolhidos ganhou.
explicacao: Lewis Terman, psicólogo de Stanford que adaptou o teste de Binet para os Estados Unidos, começou em 1921 os "Estudos Genéticos do Gênio", hoje o estudo longitudinal mais antigo e mais longo da psicologia. Assistentes vasculharam escolas públicas da Califórnia atrás de crianças muito inteligentes, e o grupo chegou a 1.528 participantes. Um dos meninos testados foi William Shockley, recusado com QI de 129, abaixo do corte. O físico Luis Alvarez também ficou de fora. Shockley dividiu o Nobel de Física de 1956 pelo efeito transistor, e Alvarez também ganhou o Nobel. Entre os mais de 1.500 selecionados, nenhum recebeu honra tão alta, como notou o psicólogo Dean Keith Simonton. Há uma ironia a mais: no fim da vida, sem formação em genética, Shockley ficou conhecido pela defesa extremada da eugenia e de ideias racistas sobre raça e inteligência, a ponto de provocar protestos em universidades. Décadas depois, o professor Julian Stanley suspeitou que Terman teria achado os dois se tivesse um jeito confiável de medir especificamente o raciocínio quantitativo, e passou a usar o SAT, um exame de admissão universitário, para buscar jovens talentos em matemática.

fontes.titulo: How to raise a genius: lessons from a 45-year study of super-smart children (Scientific American / Nature)
fontes.trecho: Beginning in 1921, Terman selected teenage subjects on the basis of high IQ scores, then tracked and encouraged their careers. But to Terman's chagrin, his cohort produced only a few esteemed scientists. Among those rejected because their IQ of 129 was too low to make the cut was William Shockley, the Nobel-prizewinning co-inventor of the transistor. Physicist Luis Alvarez, another Nobel winner, was also rejected. Stanley suspected that Terman wouldn't have missed Shockley and Alvarez if he'd had a reliable way to test them specifically on quantitative reasoning ability. So Stanley decided to try the Scholastic Aptitude Test

is currently the oldest and longest-running longitudinal study in the field of psychology. It was begun by Lewis Terman at Stanford University in 1921 to examine the development and characteristics of gifted children into adulthood. [...] In 1916, he adapted Alfred Binet's intelligence test for the United States and expanded its range. [...] to search the public schools of California for similarly gifted children. [...] Terman gradually added subjects to the study through 1928 until there were 1,528 (856 males and 672 females).

The three scientists were jointly awarded the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics "for their researches on semiconductors and their discovery of the transistor effect." [...] In the last two decades of his life, Shockley, who had no degree in genetics, became widely known for his extreme views on race and human intelligence, and his advocacy of eugenics. [...] "He went from being a physicist with impeccable academic credentials to amateur geneticist, becoming a lightning rod whose views sparked campus demonstrations and a cascade of calumny." [...] Park, Lubinski & Benbow 2010, "There were two young boys, Luis Alvarez and William Shockley, who were among the many who took Terman's tests but missed the cutoff score. Despite their exclusion from a study of young 'geniuses,' both went on to study physics, earn PhDs, and win the Nobel prize." [...] Simonton 1999, p. 4 "When Terman first used the IQ test to select a sample of child geniuses, he unknowingly excluded a spe [...] received the Nobel Prize in physics: William Shockley, the cocreator of the transistor. Ironically, not one of the more than 1,500 children who qualified according to his IQ criterion received so high an honor as adults."

gancho: A ideia de que cada um aprende melhor no seu estilo, visual, auditivo ou cinestésico, não passou nos testes. Num estudo, alunos que estudavam do jeito do seu estilo não foram melhor nas provas que os outros.
explicacao: Existem dezenas de modelos de "estilos de aprendizagem": uma revisão contou 71. A ideia mais difundida diz que o aluno aprende melhor quando o ensino combina com o seu estilo. Em 2009, um painel liderado por Harold Pashler, da Universidade da Califórnia em San Diego, explicou o tipo de estudo necessário para testar isso: classificar os alunos por estilo, sortear o método de ensino, de modo que uns recebam o método "certo" e outros não, e aplicar a mesma prova a todos. Esses estudos quase não existiam. Nos poucos encontrados, todos menos um deram resultado negativo: o mesmo método funcionava melhor para todo mundo. Uma revisão de 2015, focada nos estudos feitos depois, achou evidência praticamente inexistente a favor dos estilos. Em outra pesquisa, quase 400 estudantes responderam a um questionário de estilo: 70% não estudavam do jeito que combinava com o seu, e quem estudava não teve nota melhor. O mito tem um fundo real. Pessoas podem ter preferências, e visão, audição e tato são processados em partes diferentes do cérebro, mas essas partes são muito interligadas e trocam informação o tempo todo.

fontes.trecho: There are many different learning styles models; one literature review identified 71 different models. [...] The panel of experts that wrote the article, led by Harold Pashler of the University of California, San Diego, concluded that an adequate evaluation of the learning styles hypothesis—the idea that optimal learning demands that students receive instruction tailored to their learning styles—requires a particular kind of study. Specifically, students should be grouped into the learning style categories that are being evaluated (e.g., visual learners vs. verbal learners), and then students in each group must be randomly assigned to one of the learning methods (e.g., visual learning or verbal learning), so that some students will be "matched" and others will be "mismatched". At the end of the experiment, all students must sit for the same test. [...] the panel found that studies utilizing this essential research design were virtually absent from the learning styles literature. In fact, the panel was able to find only a few studies with this research design, and all but one of these studies were negative findings—that is, they found that the same learning method was superior for all kinds of students. [...] A 2015 review paper examined the studies of learning styles completed after the 2009 APS critique [...] the evidence for learning styles was virtually nonexistent while evidence contradicting it was both more prevalent and used more sound methodology. [...] In one study, students were asked to take an inventory of their learning styles. After nearly 400 students completed the inventory, 70% did not use study habits that matched their preferred learning method. This study also indicated that students who used study methods that matched their preferred learning style performed no better on tests than students who did not.

fontes.titulo: Neuromyths in Education: Prevalence and Predictors of Misconceptions among Teachers (Frontiers in Psychology, 2012, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: An example of a neuromyth is that learning could be improved if children were classified and taught according to their preferred learning style. This misconception is based on a valid research finding, namely that visual, auditory, and kinesthetic information is processed in different parts of the brain. However, these separate structures in the brain are highly interconnected and there is profound cross-modal activation and transfer of information between sensory [...] Furthermore, although individuals may have preferences for the modality through which they receive information [either visual, auditory, or kinesthetic (VAK)], research has shown that children do not process information more effectively when they are educated according to their preferred learning style

gancho: Num estudo com professores interessados em neurociência, os que mais sabiam sobre o cérebro acreditavam em mais neuromitos, como o de que há alunos de "cérebro esquerdo" e de "cérebro direito".
explicacao: Neuromitos são ideias erradas sobre o papel do cérebro na aprendizagem, muitas vezes nascidas de achados científicos verdadeiros. Um estudo ouviu 242 professores do Reino Unido e da Holanda, todos interessados na neurociência da aprendizagem. Eles julgaram 32 afirmações sobre o cérebro, das quais 15 eram mitos. Em média, os professores acreditaram em 49% dos mitos, sobretudo nos ligados a programas educacionais vendidos comercialmente. Os mais aceitos, por mais de 80% deles, foram três: que o aluno aprende melhor no seu estilo preferido, que diferenças de dominância entre os hemisférios explicam diferenças entre alunos e que exercícios rápidos de coordenação integram os dois lados do cérebro. Ao mesmo tempo, acertaram cerca de 70% das afirmações gerais sobre o cérebro. A surpresa veio na análise: os pesquisadores esperavam que saber mais protegesse contra os mitos, como um estudo anterior com futuros professores tinha sugerido, mas mais conhecimento geral previu mais crença nos neuromitos. A interpretação dos autores é que professores entusiasmados com a aplicação da neurociência em sala de aula têm dificuldade de separar pseudociência de fato científico.

fontes.titulo: Neuromyths in Education: Prevalence and Predictors of Misconceptions among Teachers (Frontiers in Psychology, 2012, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: The present study investigated the prevalence and predictors of neuromyths among teachers in selected regions in the United Kingdom and the Netherlands. [...] The sample comprised 242 primary and secondary school teachers who were interested in the neuroscience of learning. [...] Participants completed an online survey containing 32 statements about the brain and its influence on learning, of which 15 were neuromyths. [...] Results showed that on average, teachers believed 49% of the neuromyths, particularly myths related to commercialized educational programs. Around 70% of the general knowledge statements were answered correctly. [...] More general knowledge also predicted an increased belief in neuromyths. These findings suggest that teachers who are enthusiastic about the possible application of neuroscience findings in the classroom find it difficult to distinguish pseudoscience from scientific facts. [...] Although neuromyths are incorrect assertions about how the brain is involved in learning, their origin often lies in genuine scientific findings. [...] Support for this hypothesis was found in a sample of trainee teachers [...] where general knowledge of the brain related positively to the ability to identify neuromyths. [...] General knowledge and in-service training were expected to have a protective effect on the belief in myths. [...] The most prevalent of these myths were (1) “Individuals learn better when they receive information in their preferred learning style (e.g., auditory, visual, kinesthetic)”, (2) “Differences in hemispheric dominance (left brain, right brain) can help explain individual differences amongst learners”, and (3) “Short bouts of co-ordination exercises can improve integration of left and right hemispheric brain function”. More than 80% of the teachers believed these myths.

gancho: Para aprender a reconhecer o estilo de pintores, ver quadros de artistas misturados funcionou melhor que ver os de cada um em sequência. Mas, numa repetição do teste, 71% dos participantes acharam que agrupar era melhor.
explicacao: Num estudo de 2008, os psicólogos Kornell e Bjork mostraram a voluntários quadros de 12 pintores desconhecidos, seis de cada um. Numa condição, os seis quadros de um mesmo artista vinham em sequência. Na outra, cada bloco de seis misturava seis artistas diferentes. Cada voluntário passou pelas duas condições, com pintores diferentes em cada uma. No teste, com quadros novos, os pintores vistos de forma misturada foram reconhecidos com mais acerto. Depois, outros pesquisadores refizeram com rigor o segundo experimento do estudo, com voluntários recrutados pela internet, e acharam uma vantagem de tamanho médio, comparável à original. Ao fim, perguntaram qual forma de apresentação tinha ensinado mais: 71% apontaram a agrupada, 17% acharam as duas iguais e só 12% escolheram a misturada, o contrário do que o teste mostrava. No estudo original, 80% também tinham preferido o agrupado. Bjork chama isso de "dificuldade desejável", expressão que cunhou em 1994: condições que exigem mais esforço e parecem atrasar o aprendizado, mas melhoram o desempenho a longo prazo. Tarefas fáceis costumam render um desempenho imediato melhor, que é confundido com aprendizado duradouro. A intercalação, que mistura assuntos em vez de estudar um de cada vez, é um dos exemplos.

fontes.titulo: Is spacing really the “friend of induction”? (Frontiers in Psychology, 2014, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Kornell and Bjork (2008) [...] In Experiment 1a, participants studied 6 different paintings of 12 different unknown artists under two learning schedules. In the massed/blocked condition, a block of six paintings consisted of six different paintings by the same artist. By contrast in the spaced/interleaved condition, each block of six paintings consisted of six different paintings by six different artists. After the learning phase, participants received a transfer test in which they saw new paintings by the 12 artists from the learning phase. [...] In the present study we performed an exact and high-powered replication of [...] second experiment with a Web-based sample. [...] The findings from the present replication attempt revealed a medium-sized advantage of spacing over massing in inductive learning, which was comparable to the original effect in the experiment by [...] Eight-seven participants (71%) reported that massed presentation resulted in most learning, 21 participants (17%) reported that both presentation modes were equally effective, and 15 participants (12%) reported that spacing had resulted in a better final test performance than massing. These metacognitive judgments are strikingly at variance with the spacing effect shown on the final test. [...] experiment (i.e., 80%) reported that massing had led to better learning than spacing.

A desirable difficulty, in the context of learning, refers to conditions or aspects of learning that require more effort, but which ultimately improve long-term performance. [...] The term was first coined by Robert A. Bjork in 1994. [...] Compared with traditional easier learning methods, they appear to make learning slower. The traditional easy tasks often show better temporary performance effects, and these are confused for more permanent effects. [...] If this delay is created through studying another task or subject, the method is known as interleaving.

gancho: Num estudo, mulheres asiático-americanas foram melhor em matemática ao serem lembradas de que eram asiáticas, e pior ao lembrarem que eram mulheres. Das duas tentativas de repetir o resultado, uma falhou.
explicacao: O efeito estudado ali é a "ameaça do estereótipo": quem pertence a um grupo com fama negativa numa tarefa pode render menos por medo de confirmar essa fama, mesmo sem acreditar nela. Os primeiros experimentos, de Claude Steele e Joshua Aronson, em 1995, deram a universitários negros e brancos a difícil parte verbal do exame GRE. Quando a prova era descrita como medida de capacidade intelectual, os estudantes negros iam pior. O tema virou um dos mais estudados da psicologia social. No estudo com mulheres asiático-americanas, lembrar da identidade asiática, associada a fama de boa em números, deu um empurrão, e lembrar do gênero teve o efeito inverso. Nas duas tentativas de repetição, uma só reproduziu o resultado depois de excluir quem não conhecia os estereótipos, e a outra não conseguiu reproduzi-lo. O efeito geral também está em debate. Uma meta-análise de 2015, com estudos sobre meninas em idade escolar, concluiu que o efeito médio relatado é pequeno, talvez inflado porque estudos sem resultado ficam na gaveta, e que o tamanho real pode ser perto de zero. O maior teste experimental, com 2.064 estudantes holandeses do ensino médio em provas de matemática, não achou efeito, embora os autores avisem que o resultado vale para um contexto restrito. Outras meta-análises e revisões, porém, encontram evidência significativa do fenômeno.

fontes.trecho: Stereotype threat is a situational predicament in which people are or feel themselves to be at risk of conforming to stereotypes about their social group. [...] Since its introduction into the academic literature, stereotype threat has become one of the most widely studied topics in the field of social psychology. [...] Importantly, the individual does not need to subscribe to the stereotype for it to be activated. [...] The single largest experimental test of stereotype threat (N = 2064), conducted on Dutch high school students, found no effect. The authors state, however, that these results are limited to a narrow age-range, experimental procedure and cultural context [...] Numerous meta-analyses and systematic reviews have shown significant evidence for the effects o [...] Consistent with the positive racial stereotype concerning their superior quantitative skills, Asian American women performed better on a math test when their Asian identity was primed compared to a control condition where no social identity was primed. Conversely, these participants did worse on the math test when instead their gender identity—which is associated with stereotypes of inferior quantitative skills—was made salient, which is consistent with stereotype threat. Two replications of this result have been attempted. In one case, the effect was only reproduced after excluding participants who were unaware of stereotypes about the mathematical abilities of Asians or women, while the other replication failed to reproduce the original results [...] A meta-analysis by Flore and Wicherts (2015) concluded that the average reported effect of stereotype threat is small, and that those reports may be inflated by publication bias. They argued that, correcting for this, the most likely effect size may be near zero. [...] In 1995, Claude Steele and Joshua Aronson performed the first experiments demonstrating that stereotype threat can undermine intellectual performance. [...] They had African-American and European-American college students take a difficult verbal portion of the Graduate Record Examination test. [...] stereotype-threat (in which the test was described as being "diagnostic of intellectual ability") [...] "that the effects of stereotype threat on math test performance should not be overgeneralized." [...] Reviews have raised concerns that the effect might have been over-estimated in the performance of schoolgirls and argued that the field likely suffers from publication bias.

gancho: A "regra das 10 mil horas" para virar especialista se apoiou numa pesquisa com violinistas. O autor dessa pesquisa, o psicólogo Anders Ericsson, escreveu depois que a regra estava errada em vários pontos.
explicacao: Num artigo de 1993 muito citado, o psicólogo sueco Anders Ericsson e colegas concluíram que violinistas de elite deviam o talento menos a dons inatos e mais a muita prática deliberada, de alta concentração e além da zona de conforto, ao longo de dez anos ou mais. O jornalista Malcolm Gladwell transformou isso na "regra das 10 mil horas", no livro "Outliers", com exemplos como os Beatles e suas longas temporadas de shows em Hamburgo. Ericsson contestou. As 10 mil horas eram a média de prática deliberada que os violinistas tinham acumulado aos 20 anos, quando ainda estavam longe de ser mestres. O número de horas necessário varia conforme a área, e Gladwell não separava a prática deliberada da prática comum. Uma meta-análise de 2014 foi além e estimou quanto das diferenças de desempenho a prática deliberada explica: 26% nos jogos, 21% na música, 18% nos esportes, 4% na educação e menos de 1% nas profissões. A conclusão foi que a prática importa, mas menos do que se costuma afirmar. Ericsson continuou mostrando o poder do treino: num de seus resultados mais marcantes, treinou um estudante a guardar uma sequência de mais de 100 dígitos.

fontes.trecho: was a Swedish psychologist [...] focusing exclusively on extended deliberate practice  (e.g., high concentration practice beyond one's comfort zone) [...] In a highly cited 1993 paper, Ericsson and colleagues conducted studies in which they concluded that expert violinists derived their talent not from innate abilities but rather from large amounts of deliberate practice over a period of 10 years or more. Canadian journalist Malcolm Gladwell drew upon Ericsson's research to establish his so-called 10,000 hour rule in the book Outliers. Ericsson later wrote that 'this rule...is wrong in several ways'. 10,000 was the average number of deliberate practice hours that the violinists had achieved by age 20, at which point the violinists 'were nowhere near masters'. Furthermore, the number of hours required to become an expert has been demonstrated to vary depending on field. In addition, Gladwell did not differentiate between deliberate practice and other forms of practice. [...] One of his most striking experimental results was training a student to have a digit span of more than 100 digits.

Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014) found that deliberate practice explained 26% of the variance in performance for games, 21% for music, 18% for sports, 4% for education, and less than 1% for professions, and concluded that deliberate practice is important but less important than has often been a

A common theme that appears throughout Outliers is the "10,000-Hour Rule", based on a study by Anders Ericsson. Gladwell claims that greatness requires enormous time, using the source of the Beatles' musical talents and Gates' computer savvy as examples.

gancho: Antes de ter filhos, um húngaro leu a vida de 400 grandes intelectuais e concluiu que podia fazer de qualquer bebê saudável um gênio. Criou as filhas em casa, no xadrez. Duas viraram as melhores enxadristas do mundo.
explicacao: László Polgár estudou inteligência na universidade e notou, nas biografias de gênios, um padrão: todos tinham começado muito cedo e estudado com intensidade. Segundo a revista People, antes de casar ele leu a vida de 400 grandes intelectuais, de Sócrates a Einstein. O experimento começou em 1970, com a premissa de que qualquer criança pode virar gênio numa área se a educação começar antes dos três anos e a especialização, aos seis. O casal pensou em matemática e línguas, mas escolheu o xadrez por ser objetivo e fácil de medir. Polgár brigou com as autoridades húngaras para educar as filhas em casa. Susan, a mais velha, começou aos quatro anos e, seis meses depois, vencia veteranos num clube de xadrez de Budapeste. Ela virou campeã mundial feminina. Judit, a caçula, foi a única mulher a entrar no top 10 do ranking mundial e é considerada a maior enxadrista da história. Segundo Judit, havia quem dissesse que os pais estavam destruindo as meninas, e um jornal americano notou que os detratores o pintavam como um Dr. Frankenstein. A filha do meio, Sofia, chegou a sexta melhor jogadora do mundo e depois largou o xadrez. Mas é o caso de uma única família, e a dúvida segue de pé: um livro sobre as irmãs se chama justamente "Treino ou gênio?".

fontes.trecho: He is the father of the famous Polgár sisters: Zsuzsa, Zsófia, and Judit, whom he raised to be chess prodigies, with Judit and Zsuzsa becoming the best and second-best female chess players in the world, respectively. Judit is widely considered the greatest female chess player ever, as she is the only woman to have been ranked in the top 10 worldwide, while Zsuzsa became the Women's World Chess Champion. [...] He has been "portrayed by his detractors as a Dr. Frankenstein" and viewed by his admirers as "a Houdini", noted Peter Maas in the Washington Post in 1992. [...] He studied intelligence when he was a university student. He later recalled that "when I looked at the life stories of geniuses" during his student years, "I found the same thing...They all started at a very young age and studied intensively." He prepared for fatherhood before marriage, reported People Magazine in 1987, by studying the biographies of 400 great intellectuals, from Socrates to Einstein. He concluded that if he took the right approach to child-rearing, he could turn "any healthy newborn" into "a genius." [...] In 1965, Polgár "conducted an epistolary courtship with a Ukrainian foreign language teacher named Klara." In his letters, he outlined the pedagogical project he had in mind. [...] Polgár and his wife considered various possible subjects in which to drill their children, "including mathematics and foreign languages", but they settled on chess. [...] "But we chose chess. Chess is very objective and easy to measure." [...] The experiment began in 1970 "with a simple premise: that any child has the innate capacity to become a genius in any chosen field, as long as education starts before their third birthday and they begin to specialize at six." Polgár "battled Hungarian authorities for permission" to home-school the girls. [...] his youngest daughter Judit recalled in 2008. "People would say, 'The parents are destroying them, they have to work all day, they have no childhood'. [...] Polgár began teaching his eldest daughter, Susan, to play chess when she was four years old. "Six months later, Susan toddled into Budapest's smoke-filled chess club," which was crowded with elderly men, and proceeded to beat the veteran players. [...] Still, Sophia, the least successful of the three, who became the sixth-best female player in the world, quit playing, studied painting and interior design, and focused on being a housewife and mother. [...] In 1992, Cathy Forbes published a book entitled The Polgár Sisters: Training or Genius?

gancho: O peso dos genes nas diferenças de QI parece crescer com a idade: cerca de 20% em bebês e 60% em adultos, segundo uma revisão. E, se todos vivessem no mesmo ambiente, esse peso tenderia a 100%.
explicacao: Herdabilidade é uma medida de população, não de indivíduo: ela estima quanto das diferenças de QI dentro de uma população se associa a diferenças genéticas entre os indivíduos. Por isso o número muda com o ambiente: se as condições de vida variam mais, a herdabilidade cai; se todos tivessem o mesmo ambiente, ela tenderia a 100%. Estudos com gêmeos e adotados indicam que ela aumenta ao longo da vida, de cerca de 20% na primeira infância para 60% na vida adulta, segundo uma revisão. É o chamado efeito Wilson. A explicação mais aceita é uma amplificação: os mesmos genes passam a ter efeitos cada vez maiores, e uma hipótese é que genes e ambiente se correlacionem com o tempo. A relação com a idade, porém, ainda é tida como incerta. O ambiente social também parece contar. Num estudo de 2003 com gêmeos de sete anos, nas famílias pobres o ambiente familiar respondia por 60% das diferenças de QI e os genes quase nada, e nas ricas era quase o inverso. Estudos posteriores tiveram resultados mistos: uma meta-análise de 2016 viu o efeito nos Estados Unidos, mas não na Austrália e na Europa Ocidental. E métodos genômicos recentes dão estimativas menores que os de gêmeos.

fontes.trecho: Research on the heritability of intelligence quotient (IQ) inquires into the degree of variation in IQ within a population that is associated with genetic variation between individuals in that population. [...] The relationship between heritability and age is uncertain, though most researchers believe that there is an increase in heritability over the course of the lifespan [...] Recent genetic research has come to more equivocal results, with estimates of heritability lower than those derived from twin studies [...] If the environmental variation encountered by different individuals increases, then the heritability figure would decrease. On the other hand, if everyone had the same environment, then heritability would be 100%. [...] Most researchers in behavioral genetics now believe that estimates of heritability from classical family studies (adoption, twin studies) increase as individuals age,. One review described a "linearly increasing heritability of intelligence from infancy (20%) through adulthood (60%)". This increase in heritability with age is known as the "Wilson Effect". [...] Behavioral genetics researchers believe that genetic amplification is most supported by the evidence, where the same genetic factors that influence IQ at one age are involved later, but produce larger and larger phenotypic effects over time. One theory proposed to explain the apparent increase in heritability values is a reciprocal effects model, where environments and genes become correlated over the course of development. [...] Turkheimer and colleagues (2003) argued that the proportions of IQ variance attributable to genes and environment vary with socioeconomic status. They found that in a study on seven-year-old twins, in impoverished families, 60% of the variance in early childhood IQ was accounted for by the shared family environment, and the contribution of genes is close to zero; in affluent families, the result is almost exactly the reverse. [...] Later studies found more equivocal results, some failing to replicate the finding in different locations. A 2016 meta-analysis found that the effects varied by country, with moderate interactions in studies from the United States, while the effects were zero or reversed in studies from Australia and Western Europe.

gancho: Desde 1927 há aparelhos para "aprender dormindo", e um estudo de 1956 concluiu que isso era "provavelmente impossível". Em 2017, pessoas aprenderam ruídos novos enquanto dormiam, mas só em certas fases do sono.
explicacao: Em 1927, Alois Benjamin Saliger inventou o Psychophone, uma versão do fonógrafo de Edison feita para ensinar durante o sono. Ele afirmava que o sono natural era idêntico ao hipnótico e que, dormindo, o inconsciente ficava mais receptivo a sugestões. Patenteou o aparelho em 1932. No mesmo ano, "Admirável Mundo Novo", de Aldous Huxley, usou o aprendizado no sono para condicionar crianças. Em 1956, Charles Simon e William Emmons monitoraram o cérebro de voluntários com eletroencefalograma e viram que o material apresentado durante o sono não era lembrado depois, a não ser quando surgiam ondas alfa no mesmo momento. Concluíram que aprender dormindo era impraticável e provavelmente impossível, e a ideia passou a ser vista como pseudociência. Em 2017, uma equipe francesa tocou amostras de ruído para 20 voluntários adormecidos. Quando o mesmo ruído novo se repetia no sono REM ou no sono leve, os voluntários se saíam melhor numa tarefa com ele ao acordar. No sono profundo, a mesma exposição piorava o desempenho. Os autores ligaram a formação da memória aos fusos do sono e a supressão às ondas lentas. Eram ruídos, não aulas de idiomas, mas o estudo sugere que o cérebro adormecido pode tanto gravar algo novo quanto bloquear esse aprendizado, conforme a fase do sono.

fontes.trecho: Although sleep is considered an important period for memory consolidation, scientific research has concluded that sleep-learning is not possible. [...] is widely considered to be pseudoscience. [...] In 1927, Alois Benjamin Saliger invented the "Psycho-Phone" or "Psychophone", a specialized version of Thomas Edison's phonograph, for sleep learning, stating: "It has been proven that natural sleep is identical with hypnotic sleep and that during natural sleep the unconscious mind is most receptive to suggestions." Saliger patented the device in 1932 as the "automatic time-controlled suggestion machine". Since the electroencephalography studies by Charles W. Simon and William H. Emmons in 1956, learning by sleep has not been taken seriously. The researchers concluded that learning during sleep was "impractical and probably impossible". They reported that stimulus material presented during sleep was not recalled later when the subject awoke, unless alpha wave activity occurred at the same time the stimulus material was given. [...] In Aldous Huxley's 1932 novel Brave New World, it is used for the conditioning of children

fontes.titulo: Formation and suppression of acoustic memories during human sleep (Nature Communications, 2017, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Accepted 2017 May 30; Collection date 2017. [...] Here, we report that memory traces can be both formed or suppressed during sleep, depending on sleep phase. We played samples of acoustic noise to sleeping human listeners. Repeated exposure to a novel noise during Rapid Eye Movements (REM) or light non-REM (NREM) sleep leads to improvements in behavioral performance upon awakening. Strikingly, the same exposure during deep NREM sleep leads to impaired performance upon awakening. [...] We can trace these neural changes back to transient sleep events, such as spindles for memory facilitation and slow waves for suppression. [...] École Normale Supérieure-PSL Research University, Paris, 75005 France [...] Human listeners were tested in a whole-night sleep experiment [...] = 20) were instructed to discriminate Gaussian noise

gancho: Num supermercado da Califórnia, uma banca com 24 geleias atraiu mais gente que uma com 6, mas só 3% de quem parou nela comprou, contra quase 30% na menor. Repetir esse efeito se mostrou difícil.
explicacao: O experimento, publicado em 2000 por Sheena Iyengar e Mark Lepper, foi feito numa loja de Menlo Park conhecida pela variedade: vendia mais de 300 tipos de geleia. Dois assistentes vestidos de funcionários convidavam quem passava a provar geleias da marca Wilkin & Sons. Em dois sábados, a mesa alternava de hora em hora entre 6 e 24 sabores. A banca grande parecia mais atraente: 60% de quem passou por ela parou, contra 40% na pequena, e nas duas as pessoas provaram, em média, quantidades parecidas. Todos ganhavam um cupom de 1 dólar de desconto, e a diferença apareceu na compra: quase 30% de quem viu 6 opções levou um pote, contra só 3% de quem viu 24. O estudo virou o símbolo do "excesso de escolhas". Mas, em 2010, uma meta-análise reuniu 50 experimentos, publicados ou não, com 5.036 participantes, e achou um efeito médio praticamente nulo, com grande variação de um estudo para outro. Outra meta-análise, de 2015, com 99 estudos, concluiu que o efeito aparece quando certas condições se somam, como escolhas complexas, tarefas difíceis e preferências incertas.

fontes.titulo: Iyengar e Lepper (2000), When Choice is Demotivating
fontes.trecho: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2000, Vol. 79 [...] store (Draeger's Supermarket) located in Menlo Park, California. [...] 300 varieties of jam. [...] Two research assistants, dressed as store employees, invited passing [...] one of two displays. On the table were either 6 (limited-choice condition) [...] or 24 (extensive-choice condition) different jams. [...] days, the displays were rotated hourly [...] wished. All consumers who approached the table received a coupon for a [...] $1-discount off the purchase of any Wilkin & Sons jam. [...] selection display of jams, 60% (145) actually stopped at the booth. [...] display of jams, only 40% (104) stopped. [...] Nearly 30% (31) of the consumers in the limited-choice condition subsequently purchased [...] only 3% (4) of the consumers in the extensive-choice condition did so

fontes.titulo: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder e Todd (2010), Can There Ever Be Too Many Options?
fontes.trecho: In a meta-analysis of 63 conditions from 50 published and unpublished experiments (N = 5,036), we found a mean effect size of virtually zero but considerable variance between studies. [...] Benjamin Scheibehenne & Rainer Greifeneder & Peter M. Todd, 2010.

A new meta-analysis, conducted in 2015 and incorporating 99 studies, was able to isolate when reducing choices for your customers is most likely to boost sales. The study identified four key factors—choice set complexity, decision task difficulty, preference uncertainty, and decision goal—that moderate the impact of assortment size on choice overload.

gancho: Na Alemanha, onde é preciso se cadastrar para ser doador de órgãos, a taxa de consentimento citada é de 12%. Na vizinha Áustria, onde todos são doadores salvo recusa, 99,98%. Mas isso não garante mais transplantes.
explicacao: É um exemplo do "efeito padrão": a opção que vale para quem não faz nada tende a ser a mais escolhida. Os dois países têm cultura e desenvolvimento econômico muito parecidos; muda a regra. No sistema de adesão, ninguém é doador até se registrar. No de consentimento presumido, todos são, a menos que peçam para sair. Há várias explicações para a força do padrão: escolher dá trabalho, sair dele tem custos, e ele pode ser lido como uma recomendação de quem fez a regra. Ele muda até o peso moral da escolha: sob o consentimento presumido, recusar-se a doar é visto como falha moral maior. Só que consentimento no papel não é o mesmo que órgãos doados. A Grécia tem consentimento presumido e cerca de 6 doadores por milhão de habitantes, enquanto a Espanha, recordista mundial, chegou a 46,9 por milhão em 2017. O presidente da Organização Nacional de Transplantes espanhola reconheceu que a lei provavelmente não é a principal razão do sucesso do país, que depende de coordenadores de transplante nos hospitais e de UTIs com médicos suficientes para identificar possíveis doadores.

fontes.trecho: Opt-out legislative systems dramatically increase effective consent rates for donation as a result of the default effect. For example, Germany, which uses an opt-in system, has an organ donation consent rate of 12% among its population. In contrast, Austria, a country with a very similar culture and economic development, but which uses an opt-out system, has a consent rate of 99.98%. [...] Because of public policies, cultural, infrastructural and other factors, presumed consent or opt-out models do not always translate directly into higher effective donation rates. [...] Some countries with an opt-out system, like Spain (40.2 donors per million inhabitants), Croatia (40.2 donors/million) or Belgium (31.6 donors/million) have high donor rates, however some countries such as Greece (6 donors/million) maintain low donor rates even with this system. The president of the Spanish National Transplant Organisation has acknowledged that Spain's legislative approach is likely not the primary reason for the country's success in increasing the donor rates, starting in the 1990s. [...] intensive care units (ICUs) must be staffed with enough doctors to maximize the identification of potential donors [...] The characteristic that enables the Spanish presumed consent model to be successful is the resource of transplant coordinators [...] Spain had the highest donor rate in the world, 46.9 per million people in the population, in 2017.

In countries with the opt-in policy, all citizens are automatically considered as non-donors unless they actively register as donors. In countries with the opt-out policy, all citizens are automatically considered as donors unless they actively seek to be struck from the register. [...] it may involve too much cognitive effort to base a choice on explicit evaluations. [...] If an agent faces costs when diverging from a default that surmount the possible benefits from switching to another option, then it is rational to stick with the default option. [...] That the policy maker sets a default is interpreted as an implicit recommendation to choose that default option. [...] Under an opt-out policy, in contrast, choosing not to be an organ donor is perceived as morally more deficient.

gancho: Num experimento clássico, estudantes que ganharam uma caneca pediam para vendê-la mais que o dobro do que outros aceitavam pagar por ela. Outros primatas mostram esse apego, mas há quem conteste o efeito.
explicacao: É o "efeito dotação", estudado por Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch e Richard Thaler com alunos da Universidade Cornell, num trabalho de 1990. Uns recebiam uma caneca e podiam vendê-la; outros podiam comprá-la. Os donos pediam uns 7 dólares para abrir mão dela, e os compradores ofereciam, em média, uns 3. Em testes desse tipo, a diferença aparece mesmo quando o objeto chegou às mãos da pessoa minutos antes. Pela teoria econômica padrão, quanto alguém paga por um bem e quanto aceita para se desfazer dele deveriam ser iguais. A explicação mais aceita é a aversão à perda: vender é perder algo, e perdas pesam mais que ganhos. O efeito já foi visto em crianças, grandes macacos e macacos do Novo Mundo, e uma proposta o trata como predisposição moldada pela evolução. Mas há contestações. Um grupo repetiu o teste com os mesmos produtos, canecas e barras de chocolate, e achou pouca evidência do efeito em bens com substitutos, embora o tenha aceitado para bens sem substitutos. Charles Plott e Kathryn Zeiler atribuíram a diferença a falhas no desenho dos experimentos. E David Gal propôs que é inércia: sem saber o valor exato da caneca, nem quem compra nem quem vende tem motivo para negociar numa faixa de preços intermediária.

fontes.trecho: people's maximum willingness to pay (WTP) to acquire an object is typically lower than the least amount they are willing to accept (WTA) to give up that same object when they own it—even when there is no cause for attachment, or even if the item was only obtained minutes ago. [...] One of the most famous examples of the endowment effect in the literature is from a study by Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch & Richard Thaler, in which Cornell University undergraduates were given a mug [...] approximately twice as high as the amount they were willing to pay to acquire the mug [...] The leading explanation for the aforementioned WTP-WTA gap is that of loss aversion. [...] a person's willingness to pay (WTP) for a good should be equal to their willingness to accept (WTA) compensation to be deprived of the good [...] David Gal proposed a psychological inertia account of the endowment effect. In this account, sellers require a higher price to part with an object than buyers are willing to pay because neither has a well-defined, precise valuation for the object and therefore there is a range of prices over which neither buyers nor sellers have much incentive to trade. For example, in the case of Kahneman et al.'s (1990) classic mug experiments (where sellers demanded about $7 to part with their mug whereas buyers were only willing to pay, on average, about $3 to acquire a mug) [...] the endowment effect has been observed using different goods in a wide range of different populations, including children, great apes, and new world monkeys. [...] Jones (2001) proposed that the endowment effect is an evolved predisposition [...] They performed a more robust experiment with the same goods used by Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler (chocolate bars and mugs) and found little evidence of the endowment effect in substitutable goods [...] More recently, Plott and Zeiler have challenged the endowment effect theory by arguing that observed disparities between WTA and WTP measures are not reflective of human preferences, but rather such disparities stem from faulty experimental designs. [...] acknowledging the endowment effect as valid for goods without substitutes

gancho: A mosca gravada nos mictórios do aeroporto de Amsterdã, o "empurrãozinho" favorito de Richard Thaler, tem antepassados: na Grã-Bretanha do fim do século XIX, já se pintavam abelhas em privadas, como alvo e como piada.
explicacao: No início dos anos 1990, o aeroporto de Schiphol passou a gravar moscas nos mictórios masculinos para reduzir a urina que caía no chão. A ideia costuma ser creditada ao gerente Aad Kieboom, mas, segundo ele, veio do chefe da limpeza, Jos van Bedaf. Nos anos 1960, quando era soldado, van Bedaf notou que uma latrina em que alguém desenhara um ponto num mictório ficava mais limpa que as outras. E escolheu a mosca porque, disse, é o bicho em que as pessoas mais gostariam de urinar. O truque tinha precedentes: os britânicos do século XIX desenhavam abelhas em mictórios, num trocadilho com Apis, o gênero da abelha, que em inglês soa como "a piss" ("uma mijada"), e Thomas Crapper pôs uma abelha nas privadas da sua empresa. Funcionários de Schiphol relataram, em testes internos, queda de 80% nos respingos e de uns 8% no custo de limpeza, números muito repetidos mas baseados em estimativas por observação, nunca confirmados por um estudo controlado. Em 2008, Thaler e Cass Sunstein usaram o caso no livro "Nudge", e Thaler o chamou de seu exemplo favorito. O efeito dos empurrõezinhos em geral, porém, é debatido: uma meta-análise de 2021 achou efeito, mas com viés de publicação, e outra concluiu que, corrigido esse viés, não há evidência de efeito. Dados de equipes de governo, com mais de 23 milhões de pessoas, mostraram efeitos bem menores que os publicados.

fontes.trecho: In late-19th century Great Britain, people would put pictures of bees in urinals and toilets. They served as a target, but also a joke about the pronunciation of the honeybee's genus, Apis. Engineer and businessman Thomas Crapper even put a picture of a bee in the toilets his company produced [...] In the early 1990s, Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport introduced pictures of flies to its men's room urinals in an effort to reduce "spillage", or the amount of urine which spills onto the floor and must then be cleaned. Though sometimes credited to Aad Kieboom, a manager at the airport, according to Kieboom it was the cleaning department's manager, Jos van Bedaf, who had the idea. Van Bedaf remembered, during his time as a soldier in 1960s, that someone had drawn a dot in one of the urinals, and that the latrine with that urinal was cleaner than others. He suggested a fly because, he said, it is the animal people would most like to urinate on. [...] Employees of Schiphol Airport conducted trials to test how effective their etched images of flies were. The result was an 80% reduction in spillage, cutting cleaning costs by about 8%. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein included urinal targets as an example of what they call "nudging" in their 2008 book Nudge [...] Thaler, a behavioral economist, called it his favorite example of a nudge.

A meta-analysis of all unpublished nudging studies carried by nudge units with over 23 million individuals in the United Kingdom and United States found effectiveness in some nudges, but with substantially weaker effects than published studies indicate. [...] Mertens and colleagues (2021) produced a comprehensive meta-analysis. They found that nudging is effective but there is a moderate publication bias. Later, Maier and colleagues found that, after correcting for this publication bias appropriately, there is no evidence that nudging would have any effect.
In 2017, he was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to behavioral economics.

fontes.titulo: The Decision Lab: How a picture of a fly reduced washroom cleaning costs by 8%
fontes.trecho: Schiphol Airport is often cited as the source for studies on spillage reduction, but no studies have been conducted to corroborate these results. All effectiveness rates have been based on observational estimates, with no testing methods. Kieboom estimates that the savings in cleaning costs are closer to 8% – rather than 20% – assuming the 80% spillage reduction is accurate.
It turns out that in Victorian England it was common to decorate urinals with the images of honey bees. In Latin, denomination of a honey bee is apis mellifera, which sounds similar to “a piss”.

gancho: Diga que um tratamento "salva 200 de 600 pessoas", e 72% o escolhem. Diga que, com ele, "400 morrerão", e 78% passam a preferir uma alternativa arriscada. Os números são os mesmos; muda só o enquadramento.
explicacao: É o "problema da doença asiática", apresentado por Amos Tversky e Daniel Kahneman num artigo de 1981 sobre o enquadramento das decisões. Os participantes imaginavam uma doença mortal que atingiria 600 pessoas e escolhiam entre dois tratamentos. Com o A, morreriam 400 pessoas, ou seja, 200 seriam salvas. Com o B, havia 33% de chance de ninguém morrer e 66% de chance de todos morrerem. Quando as opções eram descritas pelas vidas salvas, 72% ficavam com o A. Quando eram descritas pelas mortes, o resultado se invertia, e 78% escolhiam o B. Para o modelo do agente racional, que supõe preferências estáveis e decisões sem viés, a forma de contar não deveria importar. Kahneman e Tversky usaram resultados como esse para sustentar a teoria da perspectiva, segundo a qual as pessoas tomam decisões inconsistentes conforme o modo como as opções são apresentadas. O efeito aparece também em escolhas sobre tratamentos médicos: em estudos sobre câncer, idosos aceitam mais um tratamento descrito em termos positivos do que o mesmo tratamento descrito de forma neutra ou negativa, e uma mudança na descrição pode levá-los a desfazer uma decisão já tomada.

fontes.trecho: The model includes several core assumptions: rational actors have stable preferences, access to all relevant information, the capability to analyze all possible options and outcomes, and are unbiased and unemotional. [...] Tversky and Kahneman proposed a new theoretical frame to understand decision-making in their 1981 paper, "The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice." [...] They proposed prospect theory, which, unlike traditional economic theories that assume people make rational choices by calculating risks and benefits, recognizes that people make biased or inconsistent decisions in real life based on how options are presented—or, in other words, framed. [...] the Asian disease problem: participants were asked to choose between two treatments. [...] Participants were asked to choose between two treatments for 600 people affected by a deadly disease. Treatment A was predicted to result in 400 deaths, whereas treatment B had a 33% chance that no one would die but a 66% chance that everyone would die. This choice was then presented to participants either with positive framing, i.e. how many people would live, or with negative framing, i.e. how many people would die. Treatment A was chosen by 72% of participants when it was presented with positive framing ("saves 200 lives"). When the question was negatively framed, the result reversed, and 78% of participants chose Treatment B. [...] older adults are significantly more likely to agree to a treatment when it is positively described than they are to agree to the same treatment when it is described neutrally or negatively. Additionally, framing often leads to inconsistency in choice: a change in description qualities after an initial choice is made can cause older adults to revoke their initial decision in favor of an alternative option. [...] When considering cancer treatments, framing can shift older adults' focus from short- to long-term survival under a negative and positive frame, respectively.

gancho: Macacos-prego que usavam fichas como dinheiro preferiam quem mostrava 1 pedaço de maçã e o entregava a quem mostrava 2 e tirava um antes. Mas há outra leitura, e a própria aversão à perda está em debate.
explicacao: A aversão à perda, uma das ideias centrais da economia comportamental, diz que uma perda pesa mais do que um ganho do mesmo tamanho. Num experimento de 2006, Chen, Lakshminarayanan e Santos puseram macacos-prego para trocar suas fichas com dois pesquisadores que, no fim, davam exatamente o mesmo: um pedaço de maçã. Um mostrava um pedaço e o entregava. O outro mostrava dois e sempre tirava um antes da entrega. Os macacos preferiram com força o primeiro, como se o pedaço retirado fosse uma perda. Em 2008, Silberberg e colegas propuseram outra leitura: com novos experimentos com macacos e pessoas, atribuíram o resultado não à aversão à perda, mas a diferenças no tempo de espera pela recompensa entre as duas opções. O próprio conceito vem sendo questionado. Vários estudos não acharam aversão à perda em decisões sob risco, talvez porque ela não apareça com valores pequenos, e Gal e Rucker argumentaram que muito do que se atribui a ela se explica melhor por inércia. Em 2024, uma meta-análise de 607 estimativas achou perdas pesando, em média, quase o dobro dos ganhos. Em 2025, uma reanálise desses dados concluiu, já no título, que a aversão à perda "não é robusta": nos estudos em que ganhos e perdas tinham o mesmo tamanho e não eram apresentados em ordem de tamanho, o peso ficou perto de 1.

fontes.trecho: Multiple studies have questioned the existence of loss aversion. In several studies examining the effect of losses in decision-making,  no loss aversion was found under risk and uncertainty. There are several explanations for these findings: one is that loss aversion does not exist in small payoff magnitudes [...] David Gal (2006) argued that many of the phenomena commonly attributed to loss aversion, including the status quo bias, the endowment effect, and the preference for safe over risky options, are more parsimoniously explained by psychological inertia than by a loss/gain asymmetry. Gal and Rucker (2018) made similar arguments. Mkrva, Johnson, Gächter, and Herrmann (2019) cast doubt on these critiques, replicating loss aversion in five unique samples [...] In 2005, experiments were conducted on the ability of capuchin monkeys to use money. After several months of training, the monkeys began showing behavior considered to reflect understanding of the concept of a medium of exchange. They exhibited the same propensity to avoid perceived losses demonstrated by human subjects and investors. Chen, Lakshminarayanan and Santos (2006) also conducted experiments on capuchin monkeys to determine whether behavioral biases extend across species. In one of their experiments, subjects were presented with two choices that both delivered an identical payoff of one apple piece in exchange of their coins. Experimenter 1 displayed one apple piece and gave that exact amount. Experimenter 2 displayed two apple pieces initially but always removed one piece before delivering the remaining apple piece to the subject. [...] It was found that subjects strongly preferred the experimenter who initially displayed only one apple piece, even though both experimenters yielded the same outcome of one apple piece. This study suggests that capuchins weighted losses more heavily than equivalent gains. [...] Yechiam, Eldad., and Dana Zeif. 2025. Loss aversion is not robust: A re-meta-analysis. [...] Silberberg, A.; et al. (2008). "On loss aversion in capuchin monkeys".

fontes.titulo: Silberberg et al. (2008), On loss aversion in capuchin monkeys
fontes.trecho: Chen, Lakshminarayanan, and Santos (2006) claim to show in three choice experiments that monkeys react rationally to price and wealth shocks, but, when faced with gambles, display hallmark, human-like biases that include loss aversion. We present three experiments with monkeys and humans consistent with a reinterpretation of their data that attributes their results not to loss aversion, but to differences between choice alternatives in delay of reinforcement.

fontes.titulo: Brown et al. (2024), Meta-analysis of Empirical Estimates of Loss Aversion
fontes.trecho: We examine 607 empirical estimates of loss aversion from 150 articles in economics, psychology, neuroscience, and several other disciplines. Our analysis indicates that the mean loss aversion coefficient is 1.955

fontes.titulo: Yechiam e Zeif (2025), Loss aversion is not robust: A re-meta-analysis
fontes.trecho: In a recent paper Brown et al. (2024) meta-analyzed the literature on empirical estimates of loss aversion, spanning thirty years [...] Here, we re-meta-analyzed their dataset [...] for studies with symmetric gains and losses and no ordering of items, the loss aversion parameter was approximately 1.07 and not significantly above 1.0, suggesting similar weighting of gains and losses.

gancho: Um estudo de 2011 com comissões de liberdade condicional em Israel viu 65% de pedidos aceitos no início de cada sessão e quase nenhum antes da pausa para comer. Críticos culpam a ordem dos casos, não a fome.
explicacao: Publicado na revista PNAS, o estudo deu nome ao "efeito do juiz faminto" e chegou perto de 2.500 citações. Os autores sugeriram que o cansaço mental empurrava as decisões para a manutenção da situação, e que o descanso e a comida devolviam a disposição para decisões ousadas. Nas audiências de liberdade condicional, a opção padrão é justamente negar o pedido. Poucos meses depois, a mesma revista publicou uma carta de pesquisadores que haviam conversado com advogados, um juiz e outros funcionários: a ordem dos casos não era aleatória. Presos sem advogado costumavam ficar para o fim de cada sessão, e advogados com vários clientes podiam escolher a ordem por estratégia. Uma análise posterior, com simulações, sugeriu que ao menos parte do efeito vinha da agenda: casos com desfecho favorável tomavam mais tempo e não eram encaixados no tempo restante antes de um intervalo. O psicólogo Daniël Lakens argumentou que o tamanho do efeito é grande demais para ser possível. Mesmo assim, o estudo segue citado, por exemplo, para justificar algoritmos nos tribunais e no livro "Determined", em que Robert Sapolsky defende que temos menos livre-arbítrio do que pensamos.

fontes.trecho: A study of the decisions of Israeli parole boards was made in 2011. It found that the granting of parole was 65% at the start of a session but would drop to nearly zero before a meal break. The authors suggested that mental depletion as a result of fatigue caused decisions to increasingly favour the status quo, while rest and replenishment then restored a willingness to make bold decisions. The paper, which was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, has been cited many times – close to 2,500 times by 2026. [...] A few months after the original paper, the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences published a letter arguing, based on conversations with attorneys, a judge, and other personnel, that case ordering is not random, as, e.g., within sessions, unrepresented prisoners usually go last and represented prisoners sharing an attorney may have their ordering determined strategically by counsel. [...] A later analysis and simulations suggested that at least part of the effect might arise from scheduling priorities – that cases with a lenient outcome required more time and so would not be scheduled in the time remaining before a break. Psychologist Daniël Lakens has argued that the size of the effect in the original study is impossibly large. [...] Interventions of AI and algorithms in the court such as COMPAS software are usually motivated by the hungry judge effect. [...] Robert Sapolsky uses this as an example to argue we have lesser free will than we think in his book Determined.
The default option for parole hearings, for example, is to deny prisoners parole.

gancho: Em 1914, Henry Ford mais que dobrou a diária da maioria dos operários, para 5 dólares. Não era só bondade: setores da fábrica contratavam 300 homens por ano para manter 100 vagas. E havia fiscais da vida privada.
explicacao: Em 5 de janeiro de 1914, Ford anunciou que o pagamento mínimo diário subiria de 2,34 para 5 dólares para os homens que se qualificassem. Um jornal de Cleveland escreveu que a notícia rasgou como um foguete as nuvens escuras da depressão industrial. O problema era a rotatividade: muita gente entrava e saía, e treinar substitutos custava caro. Com o salário alto, os melhores mecânicos de Detroit correram para a Ford, a produtividade subiu e os custos de treinamento caíram; os concorrentes tiveram de aumentar salários ou perder seus melhores trabalhadores. Um estudo de Raff e Summers, de 1987, concluiu que o caso se encaixa na ideia de "salário de eficiência": pagar acima do mercado para reduzir a rotatividade e aumentar a produtividade. Houve filas por vagas na Ford e lucros maiores. Mas havia condições.
