A parte paga como participação nos lucros só valia para quem tinha seis meses de casa e levava a vida do jeito aprovado pelo "Departamento Social" da empresa. Com 50 investigadores e pessoal de apoio, ele via com maus olhos a bebedeira, o jogo e os pais que abandonavam os filhos.

fontes.trecho: Ford was a pioneer of "welfare capitalism", designed to improve the lot of his workers and especially to reduce the heavy turnover that had many departments hiring 300 men per year to fill 100 slots. [...] Ford astonished the world in 1914 by offering a $5 daily wage ($161 in 2025), which more than doubled the rate of most of his workers. A Cleveland, Ohio newspaper editorialized that the announcement "shot like a blinding rocket through the dark clouds of the present industrial depression". The move proved extremely profitable; instead of constant employee turnover, the best mechanics in Detroit flocked to Ford, bringing their human capital and expertise, raising productivity, and lowering training costs. Ford announced his $5-per-day program on January 5, 1914, raising the minimum daily pay from $2.34 to $5 for qualifying male workers. Detroit was already a high-wage city, but competitors were forced to raise wages or lose their best workers. [...] Real profit-sharing was offered to employees who had worked at the company for six months or more, and, importantly, conducted their lives in a manner that Ford's "Social Department" approved. They frowned on heavy drinking, gambling, and on what are now called deadbeat dads. The Social Department used 50 investigators and support staff to maintain employee standards

an efficiency wage is a wage paid in excess of the market-clearing wage to increase the labor productivity of workers. Specifically, it points to the incentive for managers to pay their employees more than the market-clearing wage to increase their productivity or to reduce the costs associated with employee turnover. [...] Raff and Summers (1987) conduct a case study on Henry Ford’s introduction of the five dollar day in 1914. Their conclusion is that the Ford experience supports efficiency wage interpretations. [...] evidence of substantial queues for Ford jobs, and significant increases in productivity and profits at Ford.

gancho: Daniel Kahneman ganhou o Nobel de Economia de 2002 sem nunca ter feito um curso de economia: era psicólogo. Segundo ele, o prêmio teria sido dividido com o parceiro Amos Tversky, morto em 1996.
explicacao: Kahneman dividiu aquele Nobel com o economista experimental Vernon Smith, por levar à economia ideias da psicologia sobre o julgamento e a decisão sob incerteza. A colaboração com Tversky começou em 1969, na Universidade Hebraica de Jerusalém, depois que Tversky deu uma palestra num seminário de Kahneman. No primeiro artigo, publicado em 1971, os dois tiraram cara ou coroa para decidir de quem seria o primeiro nome e depois foram alternando. A teoria da perspectiva, publicada em 1979 na Econometrica, virou o artigo mais citado da revista. Nesse período, eram descritos como inseparáveis, "almas gêmeas". A parceria esfriou depois que saíram de Israel, em 1978, em parte porque Tversky recebia a maior parte do crédito de fora, e Kahneman chegou a dizer que acabou se "divorciando" dele. Mesmo assim, seguiram publicando juntos até o fim da vida de Tversky, que morreu aos 59 anos. Kahneman escreveu que a colaboração dos dois foi a razão do prêmio. E, a partir de 2020, passou a viver em Nova York com a psicóloga cognitiva Barbara Tversky, viúva do antigo parceiro.

fontes.trecho: for which he was awarded the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences together with Vernon L. Smith. [...] Kahneman's lengthy collaboration with Amos Tversky began in 1969, after Tversky gave a guest lecture at one of Kahneman's seminars at Hebrew University. Their first jointly written paper, "Belief in the Law of Small Numbers," was published in 1971. [...] They flipped a coin to determine whose name would appear first on their initial paper and alternated thereafter. [...] The final version was published in 1979 in Econometrica, the leading economic journal at the time. That paper became the most cited in Econometrica. [...] "for having integrated insights from psychological research into economic science, especially concerning human judgment and decision-making under uncertainty". [...] "our collaboration on judgment and decision making was the reason for the Nobel Prize that I received in 2002, which Amos Tversky would have shared had he not died, aged fifty-nine, in 1996". [...] During this period they were described as "inseparable" and as "soul mates". After leaving Israel in 1978 and accepting positions at different universities, the intensity and exclusivity of their earlier period of joint collaboration was reduced. [...] Factors contributing to this estrangement included Tversky receiving most of the external credit for the output of the partnership, and a reduction in the generosity with which Tversky and Kahneman interacted with each other, leading Kahneman to say, "I eventually divorced him". However, they would continue to publish together until the end of Tversky's life [...] From 2020, Kahneman lived in New York City with Barbara Tversky, also a cognitive psychologist, and the widow of his long-time collaborator Amos Tversky. [...] In 2002, Kahneman received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, despite being a research psychologist, for his work in prospect theory. Kahneman stated he has never taken a single economics course.

gancho: Daniel Ellsberg, que em 1971 vazou os Papéis do Pentágono sobre a Guerra do Vietnã, antes criara um paradoxo famoso da teoria da decisão: preferimos riscos de probabilidade conhecida aos de probabilidade ignorada.
explicacao: Ellsberg se formou em economia em Harvard em 1952, serviu nos fuzileiros navais e voltou à universidade em 1957 para estudar decisões sob incerteza. Em 1961, publicou o artigo que popularizou o paradoxo, e em 1962 concluiu o doutorado com uma tese baseada em experimentos mentais. O mais simples usa duas urnas com 100 bolas. Uma tem 50 vermelhas e 50 pretas; a outra tem vermelhas e pretas numa mistura desconhecida. As pessoas costumam achar indiferente apostar no vermelho ou no preto da primeira urna, mas preferem a primeira à segunda, seja qual for a cor. É uma escolha incompatível com a teoria da utilidade esperada subjetiva: ao que parece, as pessoas não gostam de situações às quais não conseguem atribuir probabilidades. O fenômeno ganhou o nome de aversão à ambiguidade e gerou uma grande literatura a partir dos anos 1980. John Maynard Keynes já publicara uma versão da ideia em 1921. Ellsberg trabalhava como analista na RAND Corporation quando entregou aos jornais um estudo secreto do Pentágono sobre as decisões do governo na Guerra do Vietnã. Acusado com base na Lei de Espionagem, com pena máxima de 115 anos, teve as acusações anuladas em 1973 por má conduta do governo.

fontes.trecho: John Maynard Keynes published a version of the paradox in 1921. Daniel Ellsberg popularized the paradox in his 1961 paper, "Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms". It is generally taken to be evidence of ambiguity aversion [...] There are two urns each containing 100 balls. It is known that urn A contains 50 red and 50 black, but urn B contains an unknown mix of red and black balls. [...] Typically, participants were seen to be indifferent between bet 1A and bet 2A (consistent with expected utility theory) but were seen to strictly prefer Bet 1A to Bet 1B and Bet 2A to 2B. This result is generally interpreted to be a consequence of ambiguity aversion (also known as uncertainty aversion); people intrinsically dislike situations where they cannot attach probabilities to outcomes [...] Upon graduating in Economics from Harvard in 1952, Ellsberg left immediately to serve as a US Marine before coming back to Harvard in 1957 to complete his post-graduate studies on decision-making under uncertainty.

While employed by the RAND Corporation, he precipitated a national political controversy in 1971 when he released the Pentagon Papers – a top-secret Pentagon study of U.S. government decision-making regarding the Vietnam War – to The New York Times, The Washington Post, and other newspapers. In January 1973, Ellsberg was charged under the Espionage Act of 1917 along with other charges of theft and conspiracy, carrying a maximum sentence of 115 years. As a result of governmental misconduct and illegal evidence-gathering [...] dismissed all charges against Ellsberg in May 1973. [...] Ellsberg completed a PhD in economics from Harvard in 1962. His dissertation on decision theory was based on a set of thought experiments that showed that decisions under conditions of uncertainty or ambiguity generally may not be consistent with well-defined subjective probabilities. Now known as the Ellsberg paradox, it formed the basis of a large literature that has developed since the 1980s

gancho: Num cara ou coroa em que o prêmio dobra a cada coroa, o ganho esperado é infinito, mas quase ninguém pagaria caro para jogar. O enigma, de 1713, inspirou a ideia de que cada moeda extra vale menos a quem tem muito.
explicacao: O problema foi proposto por Nicolau Bernoulli numa carta de 1713. Numa versão comum, a aposta começa em 2 dólares e dobra a cada coroa; na primeira cara, o jogo acaba e o jogador leva o valor acumulado. Metade das vezes ele ganha 2, um quarto das vezes ganha 4, um oitavo das vezes, 8, e assim por diante. Somadas, essas parcelas crescem sem limite, e a média esperada do ganho é infinita. Pela conta, valeria pagar qualquer preço para jogar. Mas Daniel Bernoulli, primo de Nicolau, que morou em São Petersburgo, descrevendo o jogo com aposta inicial de 1 ducado, escreveu em 1738 que qualquer homem razoável venderia sua chance, com prazer, por 20 ducados. A saída dele foi pensar na utilidade: cada dinheiro a mais vale menos para quem já tem muito, e com essa "utilidade marginal decrescente" o valor do jogo fica finito. Gabriel Cramer, de Genebra, chegara a parte da ideia em 1728. Há também uma saída prática: nenhuma banca tem dinheiro infinito. Em 1777, o conde de Buffon calculou que, depois de 29 rodadas, não haveria dinheiro suficiente em todo o Reino da França para pagar o prêmio.

fontes.trecho: The problem was invented by Nicolas Bernoulli, who stated it in a letter to Pierre Raymond de Montmort on September 9, 1713. However, the paradox takes its name from its analysis by Nicolas' cousin Daniel Bernoulli, one-time resident of Saint Petersburg, who in 1738 published his thoughts about the problem [...] The initial stake begins at 2 dollars and is doubled every time tails appears. The first time heads appears, the game ends and the player wins whatever is the current stake. [...] with probability ⁠1/2⁠, the player wins 2 dollars; with probability ⁠1/4⁠ the player wins 4 dollars; with probability ⁠1/8⁠ the player wins 8 dollars, and so on. [...] This sum grows without bound so the expected win is an infinite amount of money. [...] one should therefore play the game at any price if offered the opportunity. [...] "Although the standard calculation shows that the value of [the player's] expectation is infinitely great, it has ... to be admitted that any fairly reasonable man would sell his chance, with great pleasure, for twenty ducats." [...] A common utility model, suggested by Daniel Bernoulli, is the logarithmic function U(w) = ln(w) (known as log utility). It is a function of the gambler's total wealth w, and the concept of diminishing marginal utility of money is built into it. [...] The expected incremental utility of the lottery now converges to a finite value: [...] Before Daniel Bernoulli's 1738 publication, mathematician Gabriel Cramer from the Republic of Geneva had already in 1728 found parts of this idea [...] The classical St. Petersburg game assumes that the casino or banker has infinite resources. [...] In 1777, Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon calculated that after 29 rounds of play there would not be enough money in the Kingdom of France to cover the bet. [...] Daniel Bernoulli, after describing the game with an initial stake of one ducat, stated

gancho: Creches em Israel tinham pais que chegavam tarde para buscar os filhos. Num experimento, passaram a cobrar multa pelo atraso, e os atrasos aumentaram: a multa funcionou como o preço de um serviço.
explicacao: O experimento de campo foi conduzido por Uri Gneezy e Aldo Rustichini, e o artigo tem um título que resume a conclusão: "Uma multa é um preço". A interpretação deles é que a multa transformou a norma social da pontualidade numa norma de mercado, de pagar por um serviço. O valor cobrado ainda sinalizava que atrasar não era tão grave assim, e a relação virou uma troca. O caso é um exemplo famoso do efeito de "expulsão" (crowding out): incentivos financeiros podem enfraquecer a motivação que já existia. A ideia entrou na economia com Richard Titmuss, que em 1970 argumentou que oferecer dinheiro por certos comportamentos, contra a intuição, poderia reduzi-los; no caso da doação de sangue, que ele estudou, as evidências são mistas. Estudos seguintes de Gneezy e colegas indicam que o dinheiro pode motivar em tarefas vistas como chatas, mas sair pela culatra nas que já são interessantes por si. O tema segue em debate: uma revisão de 2020, com mais de 100 testes, concluiu que pagar por tarefas prazerosas melhora o desempenho, e que o problema aparece quando se retira um pagamento que já era esperado.

fontes.trecho: One of Gneezy's seminal studies on crowding out was conducted in collaboration with Aldo Rustichini, and it involved daycare centers in Israel. The centers had a problem with parents who were frequently late to pick up their children. In a field experiment, Gneezy and Rustichini implemented a fine for late pick-ups to incentivize parents to be more punctual. Surprisingly, after the fine was introduced, the number of late pick-ups increased. They observed that the fine had effectively transformed the social norm of punctuality into a market norm of paying for a service. The fine served as a signal that being late is not that bad, and transformed the interaction into an exchange. In another paper with Rustichini they present a set of experiments showing that participants who were offered monetary incentives performed worse than those who were offered no compensation. In subsequent studies, Gneezy and his colleagues explored the conditions under which extrinsic incentives can crowd out intrinsic motivation. They found that when tasks are perceived as boring or uninteresting, extrinsic incentives can enhance motivation. However, when tasks are perceived as inherently interesting, the introduction of extrinsic incentives can backfire and lead to a decrease in motivation. [...] "Pay Enough or Don't Pay At All" [...] "A Fine is a Price".

the idea was first introduced into economics much earlier by Richard Titmuss, who argued in 1970 that offering financial incentives for certain behaviors could counter-intuitively lead to a drop in performance of those behaviors. While the empirical evidence supporting crowding out for blood donation has been mixed [...] A 2020 study which reviewed more than 100 tests of motivation crowding theory and conducted its own field experiments found that paying individuals for intrinsically enjoyable tasks boosts their performance, but that taking payment away after it is expected may lead individuals to perform worse than if they were not paid at first.

gancho: Com a mão em água a 14 °C, a maioria preferiu repetir 60 segundos seguidos de mais 30 com a água a 15 °C a repetir só os 60 segundos. A memória pesa o pior momento e o final, não a duração.
explicacao: O estudo, de 1993, teve Daniel Kahneman entre os autores e um título provocador: "Quando mais dor é preferível a menos: acrescentando um final melhor". Numa tentativa, os participantes mantinham uma mão na água a 14 °C por 60 segundos. Na outra, usavam a outra mão pelos mesmos 60 segundos e mais 30, enquanto a temperatura subia para 15 °C. Depois, ao escolher qual repetir, mostraram-se mais dispostos a refazer a segunda, apesar de ela ter mais tempo de desconforto. É a "regra do pico-fim": julgamos uma experiência pelo seu momento mais intenso e pelo final. Em 1996, Kahneman e Donald Redelmeier viram o mesmo em pacientes de colonoscopia e de litotripsia, que avaliavam o incômodo pela pior dor e pela do fim, qualquer que fosse a duração. Num estudo seguinte, um grupo de pacientes teve o aparelho de colonoscopia deixado parado por três minutos a mais, o que incomodava sem doer. Esses pacientes lembraram o exame como um pouco menos desagradável e, nos anos seguintes, voltaram para repetir a colonoscopia com frequência ligeiramente maior. A regra tem críticos: um estudo de 2008 a achou um preditor apenas razoável da lembrança, e o momento mais memorável previu melhor do que o pico ou o fim.

fontes.trecho: A 1993 study titled "When More Pain Is Preferred to Less: Adding a Better End" by Kahneman, Fredrickson, Charles Schreiber, and Donald Redelmeier provided groundbreaking evidence for the peak–end rule. [...] The first trial had subjects submerge a hand in 14 °C water for 60 seconds. The second trial had subjects submerge the other hand in 14 °C water for 60 seconds, but then keep their hand submerged for an additional 30 seconds, during which the temperature was raised to 15 °C. Subjects were then offered the option of which trial to repeat. Against the law of temporal monotonicity, subjects were more willing to repeat the second trial, despite a prolonged exposure to uncomfortable temperatures. [...] a 1996 study by Kahneman and Redelmeier assessed patients' appraisals of uncomfortable colonoscopy or lithotripsy procedures [...] They found that patients consistently evaluated the discomfort of the experience based on the intensity of pain at the worst (peak) and final (end) moments. This occurred regardless of length or variation in intensity of pain within the procedure. [...] One underwent a colonoscopy procedure wherein the scope was left in for three extra minutes, but not moved, creating a sensation that was uncomfortable, but not painful. [...] patients who underwent the longer procedure rated their experience as less unpleasant than patients who underwent the typical procedure. Moreover, the patients in the prolonged discomfort group were far more likely to return for subsequent procedures [...] A 2008 study found some support for the peak–end rule, but also found that it was "not an outstandingly good predictor" of remembered experiential value, and that the happiness of the most memorable part of an experience predicted remembered happiness better than did the happiness of the peak or of the end.

fontes.titulo: Redelmeier, Katz e Kahneman (2003), Memories of colonoscopy: a randomized trial
fontes.trecho: Rates of returning for a repeat colonoscopy (median duration of follow-up 5.3 years) averaged 50.4% and were slightly higher (odds RATIO=1.41, P=0.038) for those who underwent the longer procedure

gancho: A "maldição do vencedor" ganhou nome num artigo de três engenheiros de petróleo, em 1971: nos leilões de áreas no mar, quem vence tende a ser quem mais superestimou o óleo. Ganhar é má notícia.
explicacao: Os três engenheiros, da Atlantic Richfield, afirmaram que as petroleiras tinham retornos inesperadamente baixos, "ano após ano", nos primeiros leilões de áreas da plataforma continental dos EUA. O artigo saiu numa revista técnica do setor, o Journal of Petroleum Technology. O mecanismo é simples. Nesses leilões, o petróleo no subsolo vale praticamente o mesmo para qualquer concorrente, e cada um só tem a própria estimativa desse valor. Nos anos 1950, não havia método preciso para avaliar um campo submarino: se um campo valia de fato 10 milhões de dólares, as estimativas podiam ir de 5 a 20 milhões. A empresa que errava para cima e lançava 20 milhões levava a área, para depois descobrir que ela valia menos. Se a média das estimativas está certa, quem dá o maior lance é justamente quem mais exagerou. E quanto mais concorrentes, pior a maldição, porque aumenta a chance de alguém superestimar o valor. Os licitantes espertos se defendem dando lances abaixo da própria estimativa, já contando com o fato de que vencer significa ter sido o mais otimista. A maldição não vale para tudo: num leilão de algo que a pessoa quer para si, sem pensar no valor de mercado, ela não aparece.

fontes.trecho: wherein the winner is the bidder with the most optimistic evaluation of the asset and therefore will tend to overestimate and overpay. [...] The winner's curse phenomenon was first addressed in 1971 by three Atlantic Richfield petroleum engineers who claimed that oil companies suffered unexpectedly low returns "year after year" in early Outer Continental Shelf oil lease auctions. Outer Continental Shelf auctions are common value auctions, where the value of the oil in the ground is essentially the same to all bidders. [...] Each player independently estimates the value of the item before bidding. [...] If we assume that the average bid is accurate, then the highest bidder overestimates the item's value. [...] Savvy bidders will avoid the winner's curse by bid shading, or placing a bid that is below their ex ante estimation of the value of the item for sale [...] The key point is that winning the auction is bad news about the value of the item for the winner. It means that he or she was the most optimistic [...] The severity of the winner's curse increases with the number of bidders. This is because the more bidders, the more likely it is that some of them have overestimated the auctioned item's value. [...] for auctions with private value (i.e. when the item is desired independently of its value in the market), winner's curse does not arise. [...] In the 1950s, when the term winner's curse was first coined, there was no accurate method to estimate the potential value of an offshore oil field. So if, for example, an oil field had an actual intrinsic value of $10 million, oil companies might guess its value to be anywhere from $5 million to $20 million. The company who wrongly estimated at $20 million and placed a bid at that level would win the auction, and later find that it was not worth as much. [...] the term winner's curse was originated in a paper published in the Journal of Petroleum Technology, volume 23, 1971

gancho: O Nobel de Medicina de 1906 foi dividido entre dois rivais que não se falavam. Cajal usou a técnica de coloração inventada por Golgi para mostrar que o próprio Golgi estava errado sobre como o cérebro é feito.
explicacao: Por pressão financeira, o italiano Camillo Golgi foi trabalhar num hospital para doentes crônicos e montou um laboratório simples numa antiga cozinha do lugar. Ali, em 1873, criou a "reação negra": o tecido nervoso endurecido com dicromato de potássio e depois tratado com nitrato de prata deixava algumas células, ao acaso, pintadas de preto por inteiro sobre um fundo amarelo. Pela primeira vez dava para seguir os ramos de um neurônio. Golgi, porém, enxergava ali uma rede única e contínua de fibras, a chamada teoria reticular. O espanhol Santiago Ramón y Cajal passou a usar o método em 1887, aprimorou-o e, em 1888, relatou que as células nervosas do cérebro de aves não eram contínuas. Era a base da doutrina do neurônio: o sistema nervoso é feito de células individuais. Os dois dividiram o Nobel de Fisiologia ou Medicina de 1906, mas, de campos opostos, já se detestavam. Em Estocolmo, Cajal conseguiu elogiar o rival; Golgi não retribuiu, e sua palestra do Nobel ainda mostrava parte do cerebelo tomada por uma rede de fibras. A disputa só terminou nos anos 1950, quando o microscópio eletrônico mostrou neurônios separados, ligados por sinapses.

fontes.trecho: A landmark development came from Camillo Golgi who invented a silver staining technique in 1873 which he called la reazione nera (black reaction) [...] Unfortunately Golgi described the nervous system as a continuous single network, in support of a notion called reticular theory. [...] Santiago Ramón y Cajal started investigating nervous system in 1887 using Golgi stain. In the first issue of the Revista Trimestral de Histología Normal y Patológica (May, 1888) Ramón y Cajal reported that the nerve cells were not continuous in the brain of birds. [...] Golgi and Ramón y Cajal were jointly awarded the 1906 Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine, but the controversy between the two scientists continued. The matter was finally resolved in the 1950s with the development of electron microscopy by which it was unambiguously demonstrated that nerve cells were individual cells interconnected through synapses

Financial pressure prompted him to join the Hospital of the Chronically Ill [...] he set up a simple laboratory on his own in a refurbished hospital kitchen, and it was there that he started making his most notable discoveries. [...] he discovered a method of staining nervous tissue that would stain a limited number of cells at random in their entirety. He first treated the tissue with potassium dichromate to harden it, and then with silver nitrate. [...] against a yellow background. This makes it easier to trace the structure of the nerve cells in the brain for the first time. [...] his later works including the Nobel Lecture showed the entire granular layer of the cerebellar cortex occupied by a network of branching and anastomosing nerve processes. This was due to his strong conviction in the reticular theory. [...] Cajal and Golgi, being from opposing camps, came to hate each other and would not speak. When they arrived in Stockholm to receive their joint prize, Cajal managed to put their differences aside enough to praise Golgi, but Golgi did not reciprocate.

There he first learned about Golgi's method, a cell staining method which uses potassium dichromate and silver nitrate to stain a subset of neurons a dark black color, while leaving the surrounding cells transparent. This method, which he improved, was central to his work

gancho: Einstein queria que suas cinzas fossem espalhadas em segredo, mas o patologista da autópsia ficou com o cérebro dele. Fatiado em uns 240 blocos, ele passou mais de vinte anos em potes dentro de uma caixa de sidra.
explicacao: Einstein morreu em 1955. Na autópsia, o patologista Thomas Harvey retirou o cérebro e o pesou: 1.230 gramas. Se houve consentimento é assunto disputado; pesquisas mais recentes sugerem que a retirada foi feita sem permissão dele nem da família, e o filho mais velho, Hans Albert, só a aprovou depois do fato. Harvey cortou o órgão em cerca de 240 blocos de mais ou menos 1 cm³, ficou com parte deles e entregou outros a patologistas. Em 1978, o jornalista Steven Levy reencontrou as fatias com Harvey, guardadas em álcool em dois grandes potes de vidro dentro de uma caixa de sidra. Os estudos que vieram depois buscaram a marca da genialidade. Nos anos 1980, a equipe de Marian Diamond publicou que Einstein tinha mais células da glia por neurônio que 11 homens de inteligência comum; a diferença, porém, só foi estatisticamente significativa numa região. A própria Diamond admitiu que tinha um só Einstein para comparar; críticos apontaram ainda controles com idade média de 64 anos, contra 76 dele, e pesquisadores que sabiam qual cérebro era o famoso. Para o neurologista Terence Hines, todo cérebro humano tem algo de único, e ligar essas diferenças ao gênio vai além das evidências. Em 2010, os herdeiros de Harvey entregaram o que restava em poder de Harvey a um museu nacional de saúde e medicina dos EUA.

fontes.trecho: Albert Einstein's brain was removed shortly after his death, even though he wished for it to not be removed: he wanted his ashes to be spread in secret. [...] Einstein's autopsy was conducted in the lab of Thomas Stoltz Harvey. Shortly after Einstein died in 1955, Harvey removed and weighed the brain at 1230 g. [...] He kept some of the pieces to himself while others were given to leading pathologists. [...] Harvey dissected the brain into about 240 blocks (each about 1 cm3) [...] Whether or not Einstein's brain was preserved with his prior consent is a matter of dispute. [...] More recent research has suggested that the brain was removed and preserved without the permission of either Einstein or his close relatives. Hans Albert Einstein, the physicist's elder son, endorsed the removal after the event. [...] In 1978, Einstein's brain was rediscovered in Harvey's possession by journalist Steven Levy. Its sections had been preserved in alcohol in two large mason jars within a cider box for over twenty years. [...] In 2010, Harvey's heirs transferred all of his holdings constituting the remains of Einstein's brain to the National Museum of Health and Medicine. [...] In the 1980s, University of California, Berkeley professor Marian Diamond received four sections of the cortical association regions [...] She compared the ratio of glial cells in Einstein's brain with that of the preserved brains of 11 other males. [...] Einstein's brain had more glial cells relative to neurons in all areas studied, but only in the left inferior parietal area was the difference statistically significant. [...] The limitation that Diamond admits in her study is that she had only one Einstein to compare with 11 brains of normal intelligence individuals. [...] although Einstein's brain was 76, it was compared to brains that averaged 64 in age [...] Researchers knew which brain was Einstein's and which were controls, allowing possible conscious or unconscious bias and preventing impartial research. [...] Hines maintains that all human brains are unique and different from others in some ways. Therefore, assuming unique features in Einstein's brain were connected with his genius, in Hines' opinion, goes beyond the evidence.

gancho: Phineas Gage, que teve a cabeça atravessada por uma barra de ferro em 1848, entrou para os livros como o homem que virou outra pessoa. Mas depois ele passou anos guiando diligências de seis cavalos no Chile.
explicacao: Em 13 de setembro de 1848, Gage chefiava uma turma que abria caminho para uma ferrovia em Vermont, nos EUA. A pólvora explodiu antes da hora e disparou a barra de ferro que ele usava para socar a carga no buraco da rocha: 1,1 metro de comprimento e 6 quilos. A barra entrou pelo rosto, passou por trás do olho esquerdo e saiu pelo alto do crânio, destruindo boa parte do lobo frontal esquerdo. Ele sobreviveu. O médico John Harlow descreveu o antigo capataz exemplar como inconstante, impaciente e dado a palavrões, a ponto de os amigos dizerem que ele "não era mais o Gage". O caso virou presença fixa nos cursos de neurologia e psicologia, mas os relatos científicos e populares quase sempre exageraram e distorceram essas mudanças. Os registros contam outra história. Em 1852, Gage foi contratado para guiar diligências no Chile, na rota entre Valparaíso e Santiago, com seis cavalos, jornadas de 13 horas por estradas ruins e passageiros para atender. Um médico americano que o conheceu lá em 1858 e 1859 o descreveu com boa saúde e sem nenhum prejuízo das faculdades mentais. Para o psicólogo Malcolm Macmillan e outros, as mudanças mais graves teriam sido temporárias, e a rotina do trabalho pode ter ajudado na recuperação. Gage morreu em 1860, depois de crises epilépticas.

fontes.trecho: was an American railroad construction foreman remembered for his improbable[B1] survival of an accident in which a large iron rod was driven completely through his head, destroying much of his brain's left frontal lobe [...] friends saw him (for a time at least) as "no longer Gage". [...] Gage is a fixture in the curricula of neurology, psychology, and neuroscience [...] Historically, both scientific and popular accounts of Gage have almost always severely exaggerated and distorted his behavioral changes, frequently contradicting the known facts. A report of Gage's physical and mental condition shortly before his death implies that his most serious mental changes were temporary, so that in later life he was far more functional, and socially far better adapted, than in the years immediately following his accident. A social recovery hypothesis suggests that his work as a stagecoach driver in Chile fostered this recovery by providing daily structure that allowed him to regain lost social and personal skills. [...] On September 13, 1848, Gage was directing a work gang blasting rock while preparing the roadbed for the Rutland & Burlington Railroad south of the village of Cavendish, Vermont. [...] the tamping iron sparked against the rock and (possibly because the sand had been omitted) the powder prematurely exploded. [...] three feet seven inches (1.1 m) long, and weighing 13+1⁄4 pounds (6.0 kg) [...] it passed behind the left eye, through the left side of the brain, then completely out the top of the skull through the frontal bone. [...] In August 1852, Gage was invited to Chile to work as a long-distance stagecoach driver there, "caring for horses, and often driving a coach heavily laden and drawn by six horses" on the Valparaíso–Santiago route. [...] In February 1860, Gage began to have epileptic seizures. [...] He is fitful, irreverent, indulging at times in the grossest profanity (which was not previously his custom), manifesting but little deference for his fellows, impatient of restraint or advice when it conflicts with his desires [...] In 1860, an American physician who had known Gage in Chile in 1858 and 1859 described him as still "engaged in stage driving [and] in the enjoyment of good health, with no impairment whatever of his mental faculties". [...] Macmillan writes that this conclusion is reinforced by the responsibilities and challenges associated with stagecoach work such as that done by Gage in Chile [...] But above all, they had to have the kind of personality that enabled them to get on well with their passengers. [...] A day's work for Gage meant "a 13-hour journey over 100 miles [160 km] of poor roads

gancho: Por volta de 1969, a "célula da avó", um neurônio que reconheceria só a sua avó, era piada de aula. Em 2005, registros em pacientes acordados acharam neurônios que disparavam para fotos de Jennifer Aniston.
explicacao: Por volta de 1969, o cientista cognitivo Jerry Lettvin contava aos alunos do MIT uma anedota inventada: um neurocirurgião teria achado no cérebro milhares de "células da mãe", que só respondiam à mãe, e as teria removido do personagem Portnoy, do romance de Philip Roth, curando sua obsessão materna. Daí veio a "célula da avó", ideia que de início servia mais para piadas e para ser derrubada nos livros: um único neurônio dedicado a um único rosto parecia impraticável. Em 2005, a piada ganhou outra cara. Pesquisadores da Universidade da Califórnia em Los Angeles e do Caltech, entre eles o neurocirurgião Itzhak Fried e seu orientando Rodrigo Quian Quiroga, registraram neurônios isolados em pacientes com epilepsia, plenamente conscientes, enquanto viam fotos de celebridades. Certos neurônios disparavam para uma pessoa específica, como Jennifer Aniston ou Bill Clinton. Um neurônio ligado a Halle Berry respondia a imagens dela e também ao nome "Halle Berry", e não a fotos de várias outras atrizes. Isso não prova que exista uma célula exclusiva para cada pessoa: o neurônio estudado provavelmente não era o único a responder àquele conceito. Os próprios pesquisadores falam em codificação esparsa, em que poucos neurônios, e não um só, representam cada pessoa ou objeto.

fontes.trecho: The grandmother cell, sometimes called the "Jennifer Aniston neuron", is a hypothetical neuron that represents a complex but specific concept or object. [...] Rather than serving as a serious hypothesis, the "grandmother cell" concept was initially largely used in jokes and came to be used as a "straw man" or "foil" for a discussion of ensemble theories in introductory textbooks. [...] Around 1969, Lettvin introduced the term "grandmother cell" in a course he was teaching at MIT, telling a fictitious anecdote about a neurosurgeon who had discovered a group of "mother cells" in the brain that "responded uniquely only to a mother [...] the neurosurgeon went on to remove (ablate) all these "several thousand separate neurons" from the brain of Portnoy, the title character of Philip Roth's 1969 novel Portnoy's Complaint, thus curing him from his obsession with his mother [...] the term had "become a shorthand for invoking all of the overwhelming practical arguments against a one-to-one object coding scheme. No one wants to be accused of believing in grandmother cells." However, in that year UCLA neurosurgeons Itzhak Fried, mentee Rodrigo Quian Quiroga and others published findings on what they would come to call the "Jennifer Aniston neuron". After operating on patients who experience epileptic seizures, the researchers showed photos of celebrities like Jennifer Aniston. The patients, who were fully conscious, often had a particular neuron fire, suggesting that the brain has Aniston-specific neurons. [...] In 2005, a UCLA and Caltech study found evidence of different cells that fire in response to particular people, such as Bill Clinton or Jennifer Aniston. A neuron for Halle Berry, for example, might respond "to the concept, the abstract entity, of Halle Berry", and would fire not only for images of Halle Berry, but also to the actual name "Halle Berry". However, there is no suggestion in that study that only the cell being monitored responded to that concept, nor was it suggested that no other actress would cause that cell to respond (although several other presented images of actresses did not cause it to respond). The researchers believe that they have found evidence for sparseness, rather than for grandmother cells.

gancho: O impulso nervoso foi decifrado num nervo de lula: sem a capa isolante dos nossos nervos, ela compensa com um axônio de até 1,5 mm, largo o bastante para receber eletrodos por dentro.
explicacao: Lulas escapam com um jato d'água, expelido por contrações rápidas do corpo, e quem dispara essas contrações é um axônio enorme, em geral com cerca de 0,5 mm de diâmetro e às vezes 1,5 mm. Sinais correm mais rápido em fibras largas, e esse axônio não tem mielina, a capa que acelera a condução nos nervos: o diâmetro grande é o jeito de a lula ganhar velocidade na fuga. Para quem estudava nervos, era um presente. Em julho de 1939, no laboratório de biologia marinha de Plymouth, na Inglaterra, Alan Hodgkin e Andrew Huxley enfiaram uma cânula fina no axônio de lulas e registraram potenciais de ação de dentro da fibra nervosa. Mandaram uma nota à Nature pouco antes da Segunda Guerra, e a pesquisa parou: Hodgkin foi trabalhar com radar, e Huxley, com o controle por radar de canhões antiaéreos. Na volta, com aparelhos que eles mesmos construíram e a técnica do grampo de voltagem, mediram as correntes de íons através da membrana. Em 1952 publicaram um modelo matemático: o impulso corre pela membrana como uma onda de sódio entrando e potássio saindo. O modelo serviu de base à maioria dos modelos de neurônio nas quatro décadas seguintes e rendeu aos dois o Nobel de 1963, dividido com John Eccles.

fontes.trecho: The squid giant axon is the very large (up to 1.5 mm in diameter; typically around 0.5 mm) axon that controls part of the water jet propulsion system in squid. [...] through which water can be rapidly expelled by the fast contractions of the body wall muscles of the animal. This contraction is initiated by action potentials in the giant axon. Action potentials travel faster in an axon with a large diameter than a smaller one, and squid have evolved the giant axon to improve the speed of their escape response. [...] In their Nobel Prize–winning work uncovering ionic mechanism of action potentials, Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley performed experiments on the squid giant axon. [...] it allowed them to insert voltage clamp electrodes inside the lumen of the axon. While the squid axon is very large in diameter, it is unmyelinated, which decreases the conduction velocity substantially.

He moved all his equipment to the Plymouth Marine Laboratory in July 1939. There, he and Huxley managed to insert a fine cannula into the giant axon of squids and record action potentials from inside the nerve fibre. They sent a short note of their success to  Nature just before the outbreak of World War II. [...] he transferred to the Telecommunications Research Establishment (TRE) where he worked on the development of centimetric radar [...] they used a technique of electrophysiology, known as the voltage clamp to measure ionic currents through the membranes of squid axons [...] was an English physiologist and biophysicist who shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Andrew Huxley and John Eccles.

They made their discovery from the giant axon of the Atlantic squid. [...] Then World War II broke out, and their research was abandoned. Huxley was recruited by the British Anti-Aircraft Command, where he worked on radar control of anti-aircraft guns. [...] Continuing their work in Plymouth, they were, within six years, able to solve the problem using equipment they built themselves. The solution was that nerve impulses, or action potentials, do not travel down the core of the fiber, but rather along the outer membrane of the fiber as cascading waves of sodium ions diffusing inward on a rising pulse and potassium ions diffusing out on a falling edge of a pulse. [...] This model forms the basis of most of the models used in neurobiology during the following four decades.

Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley described the model in 1952 to explain the ionic mechanisms underlying the initiation and propagation of action potentials in the squid giant axon. They received the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work.
The myelin sheath insulates the nerve fiber from the extracellular fluid and speeds up signal conduction along the nerve fiber.

gancho: Testes de bombas atômicas deixaram carbono-14 extra em quem viveu nas décadas seguintes. Com essa marca, cientistas concluíram que o cérebro adulto ganha neurônios. Em 2018, um estudo não os achou, e o debate segue.
explicacao: Durante muito tempo se acreditou que nascemos com um número fixo de neurônios e que não dá para ganhar novos depois do nascimento, como resume Jonas Frisén, do Instituto Karolinska, na Suécia. O grupo dele achou um jeito engenhoso de medir isso. Os testes nucleares feitos ao ar livre até 1963 quase dobraram a concentração de carbono-14 na atmosfera, e essa marca passou aos tecidos de todos os seres vivos da época; como ela vem caindo uns 4% ao ano desde então, a quantidade dentro de uma célula indica quando ela se formou. Num estudo publicado em 2013, a equipe concluiu que mais de um terço dos neurônios do hipocampo, região crucial para aprender e lembrar, se renova ao longo da vida, cerca de 1.400 por dia num adulto. Em março de 2018, uma equipe de São Francisco examinou 59 amostras de hipocampo humano, do feto ao adulto, e viu os neurônios jovens rarearem nos primeiros anos de vida até níveis indetectáveis em adultos. No mês seguinte, cientistas da Universidade Columbia analisaram cérebros de 28 doadores saudáveis, de 14 a 79 anos, e acharam milhares de neurônios imaturos tanto nos mais jovens quanto nos mais velhos. A quantidade de neurônios que nascem no hipocampo adulto continua controversa, e o papel deles no cérebro humano segue incerto.

fontes.titulo: New neurons generated in the hippocampus of adult humans (Karolinska Institutet)
fontes.trecho: The hippocampus is a region in the brain crucial for the ability to learn and remember. In a new study, published in the journal Cell, researchers at Karolinska Institutet show that a large number of new neurons are generated in the hippocampus of adult humans – which has long been an issue of debate. To reach this conclusion, the researchers measured the amount of carbon-14 found in humans as a result of nuclear testing during the 50s and 60s. [...] "It was thought for a long time that we are born with a certain number of neurons, and that it is impossible to get new neurons after birth," says Jonas Frisén. [...] In the Cell study the researchers show that more than one-third of the neurons in the hippocampus are regularly renewed trough out life. Each day, about 1,400 neurons are being born in the adult human brain, the rate declining slightly during aging. [...] Published: 07-06-2013

The bomb pulse is the sudden increase of carbon-14 (14C) in Earth's atmosphere due to the hundreds of above-ground nuclear tests that started in 1945 and intensified after 1950 until 1963 [...] These blasts were followed by an almost doubling of the relative concentration of 14C in the atmosphere. [...] Since the nuclear test ban in 1963, atmospheric 14C relative concentration has been decreasing at 4% per year. This continuous decrease permits scientists to determine, among other things, the age of deceased people and allows them to study cell activity in tissues. [...] Doubling of the concentration of 14C in the atmosphere is reflected in the tissues and cells of all organisms that lived around the period of nuclear testing.

fontes.titulo: Sorrells et al. (2018), Human hippocampal neurogenesis drops sharply in children to undetectable levels in adults, Nature
fontes.trecho: Human hippocampal neurogenesis drops sharply in children to undetectable levels in adults [...] San Francisco, California 94143, USA [...] We conclude that recruitment of young neurons to the primate hippocampus declines rapidly during the first years of life, and that DG neurogenesis does not continue, or is extremely rare, in the adult human. [...] We used 59 postmortem and intraoperative samples of the human hippocampus

fontes.titulo: Even Old Brains Can Make New Neurons, Study Finds (Columbia University Irving Medical Center)
fontes.trecho: April 5, 2018 [...] A recent study of human brains was also unable to find new neurons in adult brains. [...] Boldrini and Mann's team used a combination of molecular probes and mathematical modeling to track neurogenesis in brains from 28 healthy donors ranging in age from 14 to 79 years old. [...] "We found there were on the order of thousands of neuroprogenitor cells and immature neurons both in the youngest and the oldest people analyzed," said Boldrini.
The numbers of neurons born in the human adult hippocampus remains controversial [...] The role of new neurons in human adult brain function thus remains unclear.

gancho: O primeiro mapa completo das ligações de um sistema nervoso, o de um verme com 302 neurônios, saiu em 1986, traçado à mão. O do cérebro de uma mosca, com uns 130 mil, exigiu IA e um mutirão de revisores.
explicacao: O verme Caenorhabditis elegans tem menos de 1 mm e um sistema nervoso com 302 neurônios e cerca de 5 mil conexões. Foi o primeiro animal a ter o conectoma, o "diagrama de fiação" dos neurônios, reconstruído por completo, a partir da anotação manual de imagens de microscópio eletrônico publicada por John White, Sydney Brenner e colegas em 1986. Em 2019, com outra técnica, o mapa foi refeito e ganhou 1.500 sinapses que tinham escapado. A mosca-das-frutas pedia outra escala. Um volume com o cérebro inteiro de uma fêmea foi fotografado em 2017, mas os programas da época não davam conta de reconstruí-lo. Em 2023, redes neurais artificiais separaram automaticamente os neurônios e acharam as sinapses, e um grande esforço coletivo de neurocientistas, o FlyWire, corrigiu os erros à mão. O resultado tem cerca de 50 milhões de sinapses químicas entre uns 130 mil neurônios. Mesmo assim, o mapa sozinho não basta para simular a mosca: faltam as junções elétricas entre neurônios, os neuromoduladores, os hormônios e o papel da glia. E, ao comparar conectomas de moscas diferentes, os pesquisadores viram que os tipos de célula e as ligações fortes se repetem, mas o peso das conexões varia surpreendentemente de um animal para outro.

fontes.trecho: Caenorhabditis elegans., commonly referred to as C. Elegans, is a small (<1 mm) nematode (or roundworm). It has a very small nervous system with 302 neurons and about 5000 synaptic connections [...] It was the first animal with a fully reconstructed synaptic connectome [...] The C. elegans connectome reconstruction began with manual annotation of electron micrographs, published by White, Brenner et al., in 1986.

In 2019 the connectome of the male was published using a technique distinct from that used for the hermaphrodite. The same paper used the new technique to redo the hermaphrodite connectome, finding 1,500 new synapses.

The available connectomes show only chemical synapses - other forms of inter-neuron communication such as gap junctions or neuromodulators are not represented. [...] In 2017, a full adult fly brain (FAFB) volume was imaged by a team at Janelia Research Campus using a novel high-throughput serial section transmission electron microscopy (ssTEM) pipeline. At the time, however, automated methods could not cope with its reconstruction [...] Six years later, in 2023, Sebastian Seung's lab at Princeton used convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to automatically segment neurons, while Jan Funke's lab at Janelia used similar techniques to detect pre- and postsynaptic sites. This automated version was then used as a starting point for a massive community effort among fly neuroscientists to proofread neuronal morphologies by correcting errors and adding information about cell type and other attributes. This effort, called FlyWire [...] This full brain connectome (of a female) contains roughly 5x10^7 chemical synapses between ~130,000 neurons. [...] Comparison of these distinct, adult Drosophila connectomes showed that cell type counts and strong connections were largely stable, but connection weights were surprisingly variable within and across animals. [...] A natural question is whether the connectome will allow simulation of the fly's behavior. However, the connectome alone is not sufficient. A comprehensive simulation would need to include gap junction varieties and locations, identities of neurotransmitters, receptor types and locations, neuromodulators and hormones (with sources and receptors), the role of glial cells

gancho: A Nature recusou o artigo que descreveu os neurônios-espelho por "falta de interesse geral". Depois, eles viraram explicação para empatia, linguagem e autismo, e parte dos cientistas vê exagero nessa fama.
explicacao: Nos anos 1980 e 1990, na Universidade de Parma, na Itália, a equipe de Giacomo Rizzolatti registrava neurônios isolados no córtex pré-motor de macacos que pegavam pedaços de comida. Alguns disparavam quando o próprio macaco pegava o alimento e também quando ele via uma pessoa fazer o mesmo, como se "espelhassem" a ação alheia. A Nature rejeitou o achado por "falta de interesse geral", e ele saiu numa revista menos concorrida. Depois, a ideia ganhou o mundo: houve quem ligasse esses neurônios à empatia, à linguagem e ao autismo, e o neurocientista V. S. Ramachandran os chamou de "força motriz" do grande salto da evolução humana. O problema é que, em humanos, normalmente não dá para estudar neurônios isolados, e quase toda a evidência é indireta, vinda de exames de imagem. Em 2009, Greg Hickok listou oito problemas da teoria de que essas células explicam a compreensão das ações e concluiu que ela nunca foi testada adequadamente em macacos. A tese do "espelho quebrado" no autismo também perdeu força: um grupo achou atividade normal desse sistema em autistas, e hoje poucos acreditam que uma falha de tudo ou nada nele explique o autismo. Ainda não há um modelo aceito de como os neurônios-espelho sustentariam funções cognitivas.

fontes.trecho: A mirror neuron is a neuron that fires both when an animal acts and when the animal observes the same action performed by another. [...] To date, no widely accepted neural or computational models have been put forward to describe how mirror neuron activity supports cognitive functions. [...] In the 1980s and 1990s, neurophysiologists Giacomo Rizzolatti, Giuseppe Di Pellegrino, Luciano Fadiga, Leonardo Fogassi, and Vittorio Gallese at the University of Parma placed electrodes in the ventral premotor cortex of the macaque monkey [...] They found that some neurons responded when the monkey observed a person picking up a piece of food, and also when the monkey itself picked up the food. The discovery was initially submitted to Nature, but was rejected for its "lack of general interest" before being published in a less competitive journal. [...] It is not normally possible to study single neurons in the human brain, so most evidence for mirror neurons in humans is indirect. [...] Iacoboni has argued that mirror neurons are the neural basis of the human capacity for emotions such as empathy. [...] It has also been proposed that problems with the mirror neuron system may underlie cognitive disorders, particularly autism. [...] Dinstein and colleagues found normal mirror neuron activity in people with autism using fMRI. [...] Today, very few people believe an all-or-nothing problem with the mirror system can underlie autism. [...] This has led to suggestions that human language evolved from a gesture performance/understanding system implemented in mirror neurons. [...] In 2009, Greg Hickok published an extensive argument against the claim that mirror neurons are involved in action-understanding: "Eight Problems for the Mirror Neuron Theory of Action Understanding in Monkeys and Humans." [...] the proposal has never been adequately tested in monkeys [...] Heyes rejects the theory advanced by V.S. Ramachandran that mirror neurons have been "the driving force behind the great leap forward in human evolution."

gancho: O mito de que usamos só 10% do cérebro ganhou força com a autoajuda: em 1936, o prefácio de "Como Fazer Amigos e Influenciar Pessoas" atribuiu a um psicólogo de Harvard uma porcentagem falsamente precisa.
explicacao: Uma das origens prováveis está no psicólogo William James, de Harvard. Depois de experiências feitas nos anos 1890, ele passou a dizer em palestras que as pessoas só alcançam uma fração do seu potencial mental, uma afirmação plausível. Há outras explicações, como leituras erradas de pesquisas neurológicas antigas. A ideia circulou no movimento de autoajuda dos anos 1920, e o World Almanac de 1929 já dizia que cientistas e psicólogos garantiam que usamos só uns 10% da capacidade cerebral. Em 1936, o radialista Lowell Thomas, no prefácio do livro de Dale Carnegie, escreveu que James costumava dizer que o homem médio desenvolve só 10% de sua capacidade mental latente. A neurociência não deixa espaço para isso. Quase não há área do cérebro que possa ser lesada sem perda de alguma habilidade, e exames de imagem mostram todas as regiões com alguma atividade, até durante o sono. O órgão também é caro: corresponde a cerca de 2% do peso do corpo, mas pode consumir até 20% da energia, mais que qualquer outro. Se a maior parte dele fosse inútil, cérebros menores e mais eficientes teriam levado vantagem na seleção natural. E usar tudo de uma vez não seria desejável: atividade descontrolada em todo o cérebro quase certamente provocaria uma crise epiléptica.

fontes.titulo: Ten percent of the brain myth
fontes.trecho: A likely origin for the "10% myth" is the reserve energy theories of Harvard psychologists William James and Boris Sidis. In the 1890s, they tested the theory in the accelerated raising of the child prodigy William Sidis. Thereafter, James told lecture audiences that people only meet a fraction of their full mental potential, which is a plausible claim. The concept gained currency by circulating within the self-help movement of the 1920s; for example, the 1929 World Almanac states "There is NO LIMIT to what the human brain can accomplish. Scientists and psychologists tell us we use only about TEN PERCENT of our brain power." [...] In 1936, American writer and broadcaster Lowell Thomas popularized the idea, in a foreword to Dale Carnegie's How to Win Friends and Influence People, by including the falsely precise percentage: "Professor William James of Harvard used to say that the average man develops only ten percent of his latent mental ability". [...] Instead, there is almost no area of the brain that can be damaged without loss of abilities. [...] They reveal that even during sleep, all parts of the brain show some level of activity. [...] It can require up to 20 percent of the body's energy—more than any other organ—despite making up only 2 percent of the human body weight. If most of it were unnecessary, there would be a large survival advantage to humans with smaller, more efficient brains. [...] writes that using all of one's brain would not be desirable either. Such unfettered activity would almost certainly trigger an epileptic seizure. [...] According to a related origin story, the ten-percent myth most likely arose from a misunderstanding (or misrepresentation) of neurological research in the late 19th century or early 20th century.

gancho: Muitos amputados sentem o membro perdido, e alguns sentem toques na mão fantasma quando alguém toca o rosto. Por décadas, isso foi explicado por um mapa cerebral que se reorganiza; em 2025, um estudo desafiou a ideia.
explicacao: Entre 50% e 80% dos amputados sentem um membro fantasma: coceiras, gestos e até dor num braço ou numa perna que já não existe. O nome foi criado em 1872 pelo médico Silas Weir Mitchell, mas o cirurgião militar francês Ambroise Paré já descrevia o fenômeno no século XVI. No fim dos anos 1980, Ronald Melzack notou que a velha explicação, a irritação dos nervos no coto, não podia estar certa: muitas pessoas que nasceram sem um membro também sentem um fantasma. Em 1991, uma equipe dos Institutos Nacionais de Saúde dos EUA mostrou que o córtex somatossensorial de macacos se reorganiza depois de perder a entrada de sinais. V. S. Ramachandran propôs que o mesmo valia para humanos, mostrou que tocar partes do rosto fazia pacientes sentirem toques no membro ausente, e exames de amputados pareceram confirmar a reorganização. Dele veio também a caixa de espelhos: o paciente vê o reflexo do membro saudável no lugar do ausente e, com movimentos simétricos, tem a ilusão de mexer o fantasma, o que pode ajudar a soltá-lo de posições dolorosas; a eficácia ainda é debatida. Em 2025, porém, uma equipe liderada pela neurocientista Tamar Makin acompanhou com ressonância três pessoas antes e até cinco anos depois de amputarem uma das mãos e viu os mapas da mão e dos lábios praticamente inalterados. Para os autores, a dor estaria mais ligada aos nervos cortados no coto, que mandam sinais "ruidosos" ao cérebro. A causa da dor fantasma segue em debate.

fontes.trecho: with prevalence estimates ranging from 50% to 80% of all individuals who undergo amputation. [...] People will sometimes feel as if they are gesturing, feel itches, twitch, or even try to pick things up with their non-existing limbs. [...] The term "phantom limb" was coined in 1872 by a physician named Silas Weir Mitchell [...] One of the first known medical descriptions of the phantom limb phenomenon was written by a French military surgeon, Ambroise Pare, in the sixteenth century. [...] For many years, the dominant hypothesis for the cause of phantom limbs was irritation in the peripheral nervous system at the amputation site (neuroma). By the late 1980s, Ronald Melzack had recognized that the peripheral neuroma account could not be correct, because many people born without limbs also experienced phantom limbs. [...] Pons and colleagues (1991) at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) showed that the primary somatosensory cortex in macaque monkeys undergoes substantial reorganization after the loss of sensory input. Hearing about these results, V. S. Ramachandran hypothesized that phantom limb sensations in humans could be due to reorganization in the human brain's somatosensory cortex. Ramachandran and colleagues illustrated this hypothesis by showing that stroking different parts of the face led to perceptions of being touched on different parts of the missing limb. Later brain scans of amputees showed the same kind of cortical reorganization that Pons had observed in monkeys. [...] much of the subsequent research has been of poor quality, according to a 2016 review. A 2018 review, which also criticized the scientific quality of many reports on mirror therapy (MT) [...] concluded that "MT seems to be effective in relieving PLP, reducing the intensity and duration of daily pain episodes. [...] Nevertheless, the debate in the field remains open. [...] There is still no clear consensus as to its cause.

It was invented in the 1990s by Vilayanur S. Ramachandran to treat patients whose limb had been amputated and who had phantom limb pain (PLP). Ramachandran created a visual (and psychological) illusion of two intact limbs by putting the patient's affected limb into a "mirror box," with a mirror down the center (facing toward a patient's intact limb). The patient then looks into the mirror on the side with the good limb and makes "mirror symmetric" movements [...] Because the subject is seeing the reflected image of the good limb moving, it appears as if the phantom limb is also moving. Through the use of this artificial visual feedback, it becomes possible for the patient to "move" the phantom limb and to unclench it from potentially painful positions.

fontes.titulo: Gone but not forgotten: brain's map of the body remains unchanged after amputation (University of Cambridge)
fontes.trecho: The brain holds a ‘map’ of the body that remains unchanged even after a limb has been amputated, contrary to the prevailing view that it rearranges itself to compensate for the loss [...] For decades now, the commonly-accepted view among neuroscientists has been that following amputation of a limb, neighbouring regions rearrange and essentially take over the area previously assigned to the now missing limb. [...] a team led by Professor Tamar Makin from the University of Cambridge and Dr Hunter Schone from the University of Pittsburgh followed three individuals due to undergo amputation of one of their hands. [...] The researchers used the brain scans to construct maps of the hand and lips for each individual. [...] One participant was scanned again 18 months after amputation and a second participant five years after amputation. [...] even with their hand now missing, the corresponding brain region activated in an almost identical manner. [...] They found that it remained unchanged and had not taken over the region representing the missing hand. [...] Without an end-target, the nerves can continue to grow to form a thickening of the nerve tissue and send noisy signals back to the brain. [...] Nature Neuroscience; 21 Aug 2025

gancho: Para tirar a licença, taxistas de Londres decoram cerca de 25 mil ruas, num estudo que leva de três a quatro anos. Neles, a parte de trás do hipocampo é maior, e tanto mais quanto mais tempo de profissão.
explicacao: O exame, chamado The Knowledge, é tido como o curso mais exigente do mundo para taxistas. O candidato precisa dominar 320 rotas-padrão e umas 25 mil ruas num raio de seis milhas a partir de Charing Cross, no centro de Londres, e passar em pelo menos doze provas orais ao longo do processo, que costuma levar de três a quatro anos. A neurocientista Eleanor Maguire, da University College London, estudou o cérebro desses motoristas. O hipocampo, região usada na memória espacial e na navegação, tinha a parte posterior maior nos taxistas do que na população em geral, e quanto mais tempo de profissão, maior o aumento. O volume total, porém, não mudava: o ganho na parte de trás vinha com uma redução relativa na parte da frente. Há também evidências de que o próprio treinamento para o Knowledge altera de forma mensurável o hipocampo dos aprendizes, o que aponta para o efeito do estudo, e não só para uma seleção de pessoas de cérebro diferente. Os trabalhos sobre essa plasticidade do hipocampo interessaram cientistas e ganharam a imprensa no mundo todo.

fontes.trecho: London's black cab drivers need to learn the locations of a large number of places and the fastest routes between them in order to pass a strict test known as The Knowledge in order to gain a license to operate. A study showed that the posterior part of the hippocampus is larger in these drivers than in the general public, and that a positive correlation exists between the length of time served as a driver and the increase in the volume of this part. It was also found the total volume of the hippocampus was unchanged, as the increase seen in the posterior part was made at the expense of the anterior part, which showed a relative decrease in size.

It is the world's most demanding training course for taxi drivers, and applicants will usually need to pass at least twelve "appearances" (periodical one-on-one oral examinations undertaken throughout the qualification process), with the whole process typically taking three to four years to pass. [...] Three hundred and twenty standard routes through central London, or "runs", are defined in the Guide to Learning the Knowledge of London [...] some 25,000 streets within a six-mile radius of Charing Cross are [...] There is evidence that training for the Knowledge can measurably alter the hippocampus of trainee cab drivers. The hippocampus is the area of the brain used for spatial memory and navigation, and is generally larger in taxi drivers than in the general population.

Perhaps the most famous of these is her series of studies on London taxi drivers, where she documented changes in hippocampal structure associated with acquiring the knowledge of London's layout. [...] This work on hippocampal plasticity not only interested scientists, but also engaged the public and media world-wide.

gancho: Em epilepsias graves que não cedem a remédios, cirurgiões chegam a remover ou desligar metade do cérebro. Muitos pacientes ficam livres das crises e, mesmo assim, falam, leem e andam.
explicacao: A cirurgia se chama hemisferectomia. A primeira remoção de um hemisfério inteiro foi descrita em 1928 pelo neurocirurgião americano Walter Dandy, contra um tumor; a primeira conhecida para tratar epilepsia foi feita em 1938 pelo canadense Kenneth McKenzie. Hoje se prefere, na maioria dos centros, desconectar o hemisfério doente em vez de retirá-lo, com menos complicações. Segundo os estudos, de 54% a 90% dos pacientes ficam totalmente livres das crises. A maioria não tem mudanças cognitivas, muitos andam sem ajuda, e a maior parte tem linguagem e leitura satisfatórias. Há perdas: a maioria perde a metade do campo visual oposta ao lado operado, e pode haver déficits motores. Em 2019, neurocientistas do Caltech examinaram por ressonância seis adultos operados na infância, todos com capacidade cognitiva relativamente normal, escolhidos entre os casos de bom resultado, e acharam no hemisfério restante as mesmas grandes redes cerebrais de um cérebro com dois hemisférios, com mais conexões entre elas do que o normal, como se colaborassem mais. Os resultados de longo prazo variam bastante: a Liga Internacional contra a Epilepsia registra que cerca de um quinto dos pacientes tem trabalho remunerado, e menos ainda vive de forma independente.

fontes.trecho: Hemispherectomy is a surgery that is performed by a neurosurgeon where an unhealthy hemisphere of the brain is disconnected or removed. [...] This surgery is mostly used as a treatment for medically intractable epilepsy, which is the term used when anti-seizure medications are unable to control seizures. [...] The first anatomical hemispherectomy was performed and described in 1928 by American neurosurgeon Walter Dandy. This was done as an attempt to treat glioma, a brain tumor, and hemiplegia. The first known anatomical hemispherectomy performed as a treatment for intractable epilepsy was in 1938 by Kenneth McKenzie, a Canadian neurosurgeon. [...] This approach is preferred in most modern centers because of its lower complication rates [...] Most patients do not experience changes in cognition, but some individuals may be at risk. A visual deficit called contralateral homonymous hemianopsia is expected to occur in most patients, where the entire visual field contralateral to the removed hemisphere is lost. There is a risk of motor deficits, and this is variable. [...] some obtaining complete seizure freedom (54–90%) [...] In terms of postoperative motor function, some patients may have improvement or no change of their weaker extremity, and many can walk independently. Most patients postoperatively have minimal to no behavioral problems, satisfactory language skills, good reading capability, and only a minority of patients have a decline in IQ. [...] The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) reports that "about one-fifth of hemispherectomy patients are gainfully employed and even fewer live independently."

fontes.titulo: Patients Missing One Brain Hemisphere Show Surprisingly Intact Neural Connections (Caltech)
fontes.trecho: In the most extreme cases of epilepsy, when a patient's seizures are relentless and do not respond to other treatments, doctors may perform a surgery called a hemispherectomy to remove half of the patient's brain. Remarkably, many of these patients are cured of their seizures and possess basic motor, language, and cognitive skills. [...] neuroscientists at Caltech describe an investigation of six of these rare patients [...] The research team performed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans on the patients, all of whom received the surgeries as children and now have relatively normal cognitive abilities. [...] "Despite missing an entire brain hemisphere, we found all the same major brain networks that you find in healthy brains with two hemispheres," says Dorit Kliemann [...] The brain scans also revealed an increased number of connections between the brain networks in the patients compared to healthy individuals. [...] "It appears that the networks are collaborating more," says Kliemann. [...] November 19, 2019 [...] "We hope that a better understanding of how the brain is compensating in people who have optimal outcomes will eventually inform targeted intervention strategies for future hemispherectomy patients," says Paul.

gancho: A maior parte dos neurônios do cérebro não está no córtex, a camada enrugada associada ao pensamento, mas no cerebelo: ele ocupa só 10% do volume e tem mais neurônios do que todo o resto junto.
explicacao: O segredo são as células granulares do cerebelo, que estão entre os menores neurônios do cérebro e são os mais numerosos de todo o cérebro. Pelas contagens mais citadas, o cerebelo tem uns 69 bilhões de neurônios, contra cerca de 16 bilhões no córtex cerebral. Em muitas espécies de mamíferos, o cerebelo tem cerca de 3,6 neurônios para cada um do neocórtex, uma proporção que se mantém de espécie para espécie. As contagens derrubaram ainda outra crença antiga: a de que as células da glia, que sustentam e nutrem os neurônios, seriam dez vezes mais numerosas que eles. Métodos mais novos e a reanálise de dados históricos indicam uma proporção geral menor que um para um, com cerca de 85 bilhões de células da glia no cérebro humano, mais ou menos o mesmo número de neurônios. A proporção muda muito de lugar para lugar: no córtex cerebral há cerca de 3,7 células da glia por neurônio; no cerebelo, só 0,23.

fontes.trecho: Because of its large number of tiny granule cells, the cerebellum contains more neurons than the total from the rest of the brain, but takes up only 10% of the total brain volume. [...] There are about 3.6 times as many neurons in the cerebellum as in the neocortex, a ratio that is conserved across many different mammalian species. [...] Cerebellar granule cells, in contrast to Purkinje cells, are among the smallest neurons in the brain. They are also the most numerous neurons in the brain

While glia were thought to outnumber neurons by a ratio of 10:1, studies using newer methods and reappraisal of historical quantitative evidence suggests an overall ratio of less than 1:1, with substantial variation between different brain tissues. [...] There are approximately 85 billion glial cells in the human brain, about the same number as neurons. [...] The glia to neuron-ratio in the cerebral cortex is 3.72 (60.84 billion glia (72%); 16.34 billion neurons), while that of the cerebellum is only 0.23 (16.04 billion glia; 69.03 billion neurons).

gancho: Otto Loewi sonhou com o experimento que provaria que os nervos se comunicam por química, anotou-o de madrugada e de manhã não entendeu a própria letra. Segundo ele, o sonho voltou na noite seguinte.
explicacao: No começo do século XX, a dúvida dividia os maiores cientistas: as células nervosas passariam o sinal adiante por eletricidade ou por substâncias químicas? Segundo o relato do próprio Loewi, no sábado de Páscoa de 1921 ele sonhou com um experimento que resolveria a questão, rabiscou a ideia num papel no criado-mudo e voltou a dormir. De manhã, não conseguiu ler o que tinha escrito; aquele, disse ele, foi o dia mais longo da sua vida. Na noite seguinte o sonho se repetiu, e dessa vez ele foi direto ao laboratório. Pegou dois corações de rã batendo em solução salina, um deles ainda ligado ao nervo vago. Ao estimular o nervo com eletricidade, o primeiro coração desacelerou. Loewi passou então um pouco do líquido que banhava esse coração para o segundo, que também desacelerou: alguma substância solúvel liberada pelo nervo controlava os batimentos. Ele a chamou de Vagusstoff, "substância do vago"; mais tarde se viu que era a acetilcolina. O Nobel veio em 1936, dividido com o amigo Henry Dale. Em 1938, na noite da invasão alemã da Áustria, Loewi foi preso pelos nazistas e só foi solto três meses depois, com a condição de entregar todos os seus bens, inclusive sua pesquisa.

fontes.trecho: For this discovery, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1936, which he shared with Sir Henry Dale, who was a lifelong friend that helped to inspire the neurotransmitter experiment. [...] In the early 20th century the controversy of whether cells used chemical or electrical transmission divided even the most prominent scientists. [...] He dissected out of frogs two beating hearts: one with the vagus nerve which controls heart rate attached, the other heart on its own. Both hearts were bathed in a saline solution (i.e. Ringer's solution). By electrically stimulating the vagus nerve, Loewi made the first heart beat slower. Then, Loewi took some of the liquid bathing the first heart and applied it to the second heart. The application of the liquid made the second heart also beat slower, proving that some soluble chemical released by the vagus nerve was controlling the heart rate. He called the unknown chemical Vagusstoff, naming it after the nerve and the German word for substance. It was later found that this chemical corresponded to acetylcholine. [...] After being arrested, along with two of his sons, on the night of the German invasion of Austria, March 11, 1938, Loewi was released after three months on condition that he "voluntarily" relinquish all his possessions, including his research, to the Nazis. [...] On Easter Saturday 1921, he dreamed of an experiment that would prove once and for all that transmission of nerve impulses was chemical, not electrical. He woke up, scribbled the experiment onto a scrap of paper on his night-stand, and went back to sleep. The next morning, he found, to his horror, that he couldn't read his midnight scribbles. That day, he said, was the longest day of his life, as he could not remember his dream. That night, however, he had the same dream. This time, he immediately went to his lab to perform the experiment.
